items.title: Beyond the Falling Blocks: Rethinking public safety and responsibility around construction sites in Ghana.
items.description: When Construction Becomes a Public Risk Imagine walking along a busy street in Accra when suddenly blocks, concrete fragments, or other construction materials come crashing down from a building several floors above you. You have no connection to the project, yet your life could be in danger simply because you happened to be nearby. This is the uncomfortable reality of poorly managed construction activities. It is worse in brownfield construction projects. i.e. construction projects that involve renovating, expanding, or redeveloping an existing, previously used property, often while surrounding operations or infrastructure remain active On 21 October 2026, an incident at a high-rise development at Villaggio, near the Tetteh Quarshie Interchange in Accra, brought this concern into sharp focus. While some accounts suggested that the falling materials may have resulted from a deliberate attempt to dispose of construction debris, other reports attributed the incident to strong winds sweeping away freshly constructed blockwork. Subsequent inspections reportedly identified vulnerabilities in recently laid blockwork, while indicating that the building’s main structural system was not at risk of collapse. Fortunately, no casualties were reported. However, the incident raises a more important question: what happens when construction activities put the lives and properties of people who have nothing to do with the project at risk? This concern is reinforced by other building-related incidents in Ghana, including the building collapses reported at Avenor and Adenta in June 2026, which resulted in fatalities, injuries and damage to surrounding properties. These incidents remind us that the consequences of unsafe construction can extend far beyond the workers and structures directly involved. Looking beyond the Fence: The Construction Site Is Not an Island In major cities like Accra and Kumasi, rapid urbanisation and rising demand for residential and commercial developments have created an environment around the central business district where new construction projects are often undertaken close to existing homes, offices, shops, schools, and public roads. In some neighbourhoods, a multi-storey development may rise directly beside an occupied residential building, leaving little physical separation between construction activities and everyday human activities. Consequently, construction risks extend beyond the site boundary. Falling materials, unsecured scaffolding, uncontrolled demolition, excessive dust, vibration, deep excavations and moving construction equipment can affect pedestrians, motorists, residents and neighbouring buildings. This makes it necessary to distinguish between occupational safety, which primarily protects workers, and public safety, which extends protection to everyone who may be affected by construction activities. A construction fence should not be viewed as the boundary of a project’s safety responsibility; it should be the first line of protection between potentially hazardous activities and the public. The Legal and Contractual Responsibility Ghana has established legal and regulatory provisions to guide construction activities and protect people and properties. The Factories, Offices and Shops Act, 1970 (Act 328), particularly Section 57, addresses safety in building and civil engineering operations, while the Labour Act, 2003 (Act 651), Section 118, requires employers to provide safe and healthy working conditions. Importantly, contractors also have a responsibility to safeguard people who are not in their employment but may be affected by their operations, including members of the public. The National Building Regulations, 1996 (LI 1630), also provide for hoarding, scaffolding, temporary structures and precautions during demolition to protect the public and adjoining properties. Beyond statutory requirements, the Public Procurement Authority’s Standard Tender Document for Major Works contains relevant contractual provisions. In particular, Sub-Clause 4.8 addresses safety procedures and the protection of the public and adjoining land, while Sub-Clause 6.7 addresses health and safety arrangements. These provisions demonstrate that public protection is not merely a professional courtesy; it is an important part of construction and contractual responsibility. Furthermore, the law of tort provides another basis for accountability. Under the principle of negligence, a party may be liable where a failure to exercise reasonable care results in foreseeable injury or damage. Nuisance may arise where construction activities unreasonably interfere with the use and enjoyment of neighbouring properties through excessive noise, dust or vibration, while trespass may become relevant where construction materials or equipment unlawfully encroach on adjoining land. These principles reinforce the need to prevent harm rather than wait until someone suffers a loss before taking safety seriously. What Causes These Incidents? Construction-related incidents affecting the public often result from a combination of preventable factors. These include inadequate site fencing and perimeter protection, poorly secured blockwork and scaffolding, careless handling or disposal of construction debris, inadequate supervision and weak enforcement of safety procedures. Weather conditions, particularly strong winds and heavy rainfall, can expose weaknesses in temporary structures and unsecured materials. Poor traffic management also creates risks where pedestrians and construction vehicles share access routes without adequate separation, warning signs or designated crossing points. Additionally, excavation, piling and demolition undertaken without proper assessment of neighbouring buildings can result in cracks, settlement and other forms of property damage. Ultimately, pressure to meet deadlines and minimise costs can sometimes mean safety gets less attention than it deserves, especially safety beyond the site fences. What Should Change? Addressing these challenges requires a combination of traditional safety practices and modern technological solutions. Construction sites should have adequate hoarding, safety nets, covered pedestrian walkways, warning signs, designated traffic routes and proper separation of pedestrians from construction vehicles. Materials must be stored securely, and waste from elevated floors should be brought down using designated chutes or hoists rather than thrown from heights. Pre-construction condition surveys should also be undertaken on neighbouring buildings, with appropriate vibration and settlement monitoring where necessary. Beyond these conventional measures, the industry should embrace innovations such as Artificial Intelligence (AI) for predicting hazards and detecting unsafe site activities, Building Information Modelling (BIM) for identifying construction risks before work begins, drones for inspecting elevated structures, and Virtual Reality (VR) for simulating hazardous situations during safety training. Internet of Things (IoT) sensors can also monitor vibrations, structural movement and weather conditions, providing early warnings when safety thresholds are exceeded. However, technology must complement, not replace, competent supervision, professional judgement and regulatory enforcement. Development Must Not Come at the Expense of Public Safety The responsibility for improving construction safety must be shared. Developers must provide adequate resources for safety, consultants must incorporate risk considerations into project planning and supervision, contractors must implement approved safety procedures, and regulatory authorities must strengthen inspections and enforcement. As Accra continues to expand, the proximity of new developments to existing buildings and public spaces makes this responsibility increasingly important. The Villaggio incident, irrespective of the competing explanations surrounding the falling materials, should encourage a broader conversation about how construction activities affect the public. Perhaps the industry should begin asking a question beyond whether projects are being delivered on time, within budget and to specification: are they being delivered without placing the lives, properties and livelihoods of others at unnecessary risk? After all, the true success of a construction project should not be determined solely by the structure that stands when construction is completed, but also by the lives, properties and communities that remain safe throughout its delivery. The author, Emmanuel Adinyira, is co-founder of Adinyira Built Environment Research Foundation (AberFoundation) and a Professor of Construction Project Management at KNUST, Kumasi, Ghana. He is a Fellow of the Ghana Institute of Construction, a Fellow of the Occupational Safety and Health Association, UK (FOSHA-UK), a Professional Member of the Ghana Institution of Surveyors, and a Professional Engineering Technologist with the Institution of Engineering and Technology, Ghana The assistance of Mr Michael Abakah, a National Service Personnel at the Office of the Dean, Faculty of Built Environment, KNUST, is acknowledged.

items.title: We won’t celebrate thieves, drug barons again — Otti
items.description: . Honours Prof. Oluikpe @ 90 By Steve Oko UMUAHIA — Governor Alex Otti of Abia State has declared that his administration is deliberately dismantling what he described as a culture of celebrating thieves, fraudsters, drug barons and other dubious characters, insisting that the state must return to honouring people of integrity and genuine accomplishments. Otti, who spoke at the 90th birthday celebration of Emeritus Professor Benson Oluikpe in Umuahia, said his administration was institutionalising the celebration of excellence as a way of inspiring younger generations to pursue worthy achievements. “We want to depart from that inherited culture. It’s not our culture. Culture of celebrating thieves. Culture of celebrating 419-ers. Culture of celebrating drug barons. Culture of celebrating bandits. That’s not our culture. That’s not how we grew up,” the governor declared. He said the practice of honouring people only after their death, when they could no longer enjoy the recognition, was misplaced, stressing that there was no better time to celebrate outstanding individuals than when they were alive. According to him, celebrating achievers while alive would not only acknowledge their contributions but also encourage others, particularly young people, to aspire to excellence. Otti cited the recent celebration of five Abia schoolchildren who emerged champions at an international competition in Qatar, saying his administration was determined to make excellence, rather than questionable wealth and influence, the basis for public recognition. The governor also used his personal experience to underscore the importance of accountability, recalling how his father questioned him in 1989 over the source of the N100 he sent home while working at Citibank. He explained that he had earned the money through extra work and daily allowances, adding that his father insisted on knowing how he legitimately made it. “That’s how I was brought up. You needed to give account. But these days, people don’t ask questions. We need to go back to that time when we would ask questions. Ask your children questions. Let them give account,” he said. Otti maintained that times had not changed as much as people’s values, citing his son’s decision to provide receipts and explanations for money he had saved towards purchasing a house in the United States. Earlier, Oluikpe, while expressing gratitude for the honour, prayed that God would reciprocate the governor’s gesture. “You have honoured me; may God honour you,” the nonagenarian said. The professor, who disclosed that he first met Otti in 2013 when the latter was still a banker, described him as a humble man endowed with wisdom, saying the impression he formed of him at the time influenced his subsequent support for his political ambition. Recounting how Otti once stood up to return an award to him at a public function, Oluikpe said the gesture revealed a humility that had remained consistent in the governor’s public life. He also interpreted Otti’s electoral setback in 2015 as a divine postponement of his political moment, insisting that God’s timing had ultimately vindicated him. “I do believe that God was telling you, ‘My son, wait. This is not your time. The time will come, and when that time comes, you will make a great impact in your state,’” he said. Oluikpe, an academic who said he had always measured life by its impact on humanity, urged public office holders to embrace generosity and make their resources beneficial to others. “A life without impact on humanity is no life. The wealth we acquire without reaching or touching minds is useless,” he declared. He also cautioned against sycophancy in public life, urging the governor’s supporters to tell him the truth rather than flatter him. Responding to Oluikpe’s recollection of their first encounter, Otti said the professor’s account reflected his own understanding of the political twists that delayed his emergence as governor in 2015. He recalled that although he had won the election, he had to pursue his mandate through the courts, eventually reclaiming it at the Court of Appeal on December 31, 2015, before the Supreme Court affirmed it on February 3, 2016. The governor said the experience reinforced his belief that God’s timing was always the best. Otti further disclosed plans to celebrate another Abia-born professor and inventor based in the United States in December, describing him as a globally recognised scientist whose invention helps in accurately targeting cancer cells. He said the recognition of outstanding Abians would remain open to all, irrespective of their political affiliation, religion or place of residence. “Once you are from Abia and you are doing well, we will celebrate you,” he said. The post We won’t celebrate thieves, drug barons again — Otti appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: La maladie d’Ebola a fait plus de 5300 victimes dont la majorité en RDC
items.description: L'épidémie d'Ebola en Afrique a fait plus de 5 300 victimes, dont la majorité en République démocratique du Congo, épicentre de l'épidémie, selon le Centre de contrôle et de prévention des maladies de l'Union africaine. La République démocratique du Congo a officiellement annoncé l'épidémie il y a environ six mois, soit le 15 mai. Les spécialistes s'accordent à dire que le virus, détecté tardivement, était réapparu dans ce pays de plus de cent millions d'habitants plusieurs mois auparavant. Le virus Ebola, qui se transmet par contact avec les fluides corporels et provoque une fièvre hémorragique aiguë, a causé la mort de plus de 15 000 personnes en Afrique au cours des cinquante dernières années. La pire épidémie jamais enregistrée en République démocratique du Congo a fait environ 2 300 morts sur les 3 500 cas recensés entre 2018 et 2020. Selon les données transmises à l’Agence France-Presse par le Centre de contrôle des maladies de l’Union africaine, l’épidémie d’Ebola qui s’est propagée dans d’autres régions du continent africain a causé la mort de 5 376 personnes, dont 5 372 en République démocratique du Congo, deux en Ouganda et une au Kenya. Au total, 10 444 cas ont été signalés, avec un taux de mortalité supérieur à 50 %. L'épidémie actuelle est due à la souche Bundibugyo du virus Ebola, pour laquelle il n'existe à ce jour ni vaccin ni traitement approuvé.

items.title: Nigeria targets wider access to West African markets
items.description: … FG urges businesses to exploit ECOWAS trade scheme By Boluwaji Obahopo, Lokoja LOKOJA — The Federal Government has urged Nigerian manufacturers, farmers and entrepreneurs to take advantage of the ECOWAS Trade Liberalisation Scheme (ETLS) to expand their businesses into West African markets. The government said increased regional trade was critical to economic growth, integration and stability across the sub-region. The Minister of State for Foreign Affairs, Ambassador Sola Enikanolaiye, made the call at the ECOWAS Trade Liberalisation Scheme Sensitisation Workshop for the North-Central zone, held in Lokoja, Kogi State, in collaboration with the ECOWAS Commission. Enikanolaiye disclosed that Nigeria had registered about 3,500 companies and 20,000 products under the scheme, but said the figures remained below the country’s potential compared with the performance of some other ECOWAS member states. He urged Nigerian businesses to exploit the scheme, which grants qualifying products originating from member countries preferential access to regional markets, to increase exports, expand production and improve the country’s competitiveness. The minister identified the agricultural potential of Kogi and other North-Central states as an opportunity to develop products for regional and international markets. He listed livestock, mangoes, millet, maize, sugar, groundnuts and cashew as commodities that could be processed into value-added products for export to other West African countries. Enikanolaiye urged participants to use the workshop to familiarise themselves with product registration procedures, rules of origin, certification and other requirements for accessing preferential markets under the scheme. “Expanding trade among African countries would not only promote economic cooperation but also strengthen relationships among nations and contribute to peace and security across the continent,” he said. The minister’s appeal comes as Kogi State seeks to position itself as a centre for regional commerce, industrial production and agricultural processing, leveraging its geographical location and natural resources. Welcoming participants, Governor Ahmed Usman Ododo said the state’s location at the confluence of Rivers Niger and Benue, agricultural resources, solid mineral deposits and road networks connecting major economic centres offered significant opportunities for trade and investment. Ododo said his administration’s 32-year development plan was designed to translate these advantages into sustainable economic prosperity. He disclosed that the proposed Ajaokuta Free Trade Zone, Agro-Processing Zone and Kogi International Airport were among the strategic projects being pursued to attract investors, expand production capacity and connect local businesses to international markets. The governor also highlighted the Kogi Rebrand Initiative and Invest in Kogi campaign as efforts to showcase investment opportunities in agriculture, solid minerals, tourism and industrial development. He urged farmers, manufacturers, miners, processors and entrepreneurs in the state to look beyond the domestic market and prepare their products for consumers across West Africa, particularly in Accra, Abidjan, Lome and Cotonou. Ododo commended President Bola Tinubu for his economic reform agenda, saying policy consistency, local production and an enabling business environment were necessary to build a competitive economy. He assured that the state would continue to complement Federal Government initiatives through infrastructure development, investment promotion and enterprise support. Also speaking, the Secretary to the Kogi State Government, Dr Folashade Ayoade Arike, reaffirmed the state’s readiness to participate in international trade, describing regional market access as an opportunity to expand the commercial potential of local businesses. Ayoade identified the proposed international airport and the ongoing Lokoja International Market project as important infrastructure for facilitating the movement of goods and connecting businesses to wider markets. She appealed to the Federal Government to support the completion of critical infrastructure projects that would strengthen the state’s commercial capacity. The SSG also assured participants of the state government’s commitment to security, describing it as a fundamental requirement for successful business operations and investment. items.title: FIFA : le «very very important friend» de Gianni Infantino au cœur des révélations
items.description: Bruno Chiomento, president de la commission de gouvernance, d'audit et de conformite de la FIFA depuis mai 2025, fait l'objet de revelations concernant les avantages dont il aurait beneficie et sa proximite avec Gianni Infantino . Selon des documents cites par Le Monde , plusieurs decisions prises au sein de l'instance soulevent des interrogations sur d'eventuels conflits d'interets. a la tete de cette commission, le dirigeant suisse supervise notamment la sous-commission chargee de determiner les remunerations des hauts responsables de la FIFA. Il a ainsi approuve les avantages financiers, fiscaux et materiels accordes a Gianni Infantino et a son epouse, dont la prise en charge par la FIFA des impots du president aux etats-Unis pour les annees 2024, 2025 et 2026. En juin, Bruno Chiomento a egalement valide une nouvelle version des regles encadrant les compensations des dirigeants de l'organisation, notamment celles du president et du secretaire general Mattias Grafström. Selon Le Monde , ce texte aurait ete elabore par Gianni Rizzello, un avocat suisse presente comme proche de Gianni Infantino. Une remuneration revue a la hausse D'autres revelations concernent Bruno Chiomento lui-meme. Selon des documents internes cites par Le Monde , il est devenu, en fevrier, le seul president de commission de la FIFA remunere en francs suisses plutot qu'en dollars. Sa remuneration annuelle atteint desormais 250 000 francs suisses, un changement de devise qui se serait accompagne d'une augmentation significative de ses retributions. Cette decision aurait ete approuvee par la sous-commission chargee des remunerations, que Bruno Chiomento preside lui-meme. Les documents consultes ne permettent toutefois pas de determiner s'il s'est recuse lors de l'examen de cette mesure. Autre privilege revele : il serait le seul president de commission de la FIFA a avoir beneficie d'une accreditation pour la Coupe du monde 2026. Invite par Mattias Grafström, il aurait egalement eu acces a la tribune « VVIP », un espace reserve aux personnalites beneficiant du plus haut niveau d'accueil, notamment lors de rencontres disputees a Miami. Selon l'UEFA, la FIFA aurait pris en charge ses frais pendant plus de cinq semaines au cours du tournoi. a l'inverse, son adjoint americain, Chris Mihm, aurait refuse certaines invitations, notamment pour le match d'ouverture et la finale, afin de preserver son independance. L'UEFA met en cause son impartialite La proximite entre Bruno Chiomento et Gianni Infantino suscite egalement des interrogations sur son role dans le processus electoral de la FIFA. Le Suisse dirige le comite charge de verifier l'eligibilite des candidats a la presidence de l'instance, dont l'election est prevue le 18 mars 2027 a Rabat. Dans une lettre adressee le 19 octobre au secretaire general de la FIFA, Mattias Grafström, le secretaire general de l'UEFA, Theodore Theodoridis, a exprime ses « preoccupations concernant l'independance et l'impartialite » de Bruno Chiomento. Il a notamment demande si une eventuelle recusation de ce dernier et son remplacement par son adjoint pendant la duree du processus electoral etaient envisages. L'UEFA rappelle dans ce courrier que Bruno Chiomento connaît Gianni Infantino depuis une vingtaine d'annees. Deux sources proches du dossier ont confirme au Monde que les deux hommes avaient notamment travaille ensemble sur un audit de l'UEFA, lorsque Gianni Infantino occupait encore des fonctions au sein de la confederation europeenne. Alors que Gianni Infantino brigue un nouveau mandat, les candidatures a la presidence de la FIFA doivent etre deposees au plus tard le 18 novembre.

items.title: Édouard Philippe rejette la «primaire des démocrates», Gabriel Attal maintient
items.description: Le maire du Havre a ferme la porte le 1er novembre au 20h de TF1 a la proposition de son rival Renaissance d'organiser une grande primaire pour rassembler le centre et la droite avant 2027. Gabriel Attal, qui avait lance l'appel quatre jours plus tot pour conjurer un second tour entre La France insoumise (LFI) et le Rassemblement national (RN), a repondu des le lendemain en la jugeant inevitable. Un refus categorique du favori face a un camp disperse Invite du 20h de TF1, edouard Philippe a tranche : « C'est une primaire de la division et de la confusion », persuade qu'elle « n'aura pas lieu » car elle tenterait de « rassembler des gens qui ne sont pas d'accord ». Il estime tous les pretendants « legitimes » et renvoie le departage a fevrier, ou « chacun prendra ses responsabilites ». Au mois de février, chacun prendra ses responsabilités. J’ai l’habitude de prendre les miennes. En attendant, je continue d’aller à la rencontre des Français pour les écouter et leur dire ce que je propose. https://t.co/yAN9HNvEsH — Edouard Philippe (@EPhilippe_LH) November 1, 2026 Gabriel Attal a retorque le 2 novembre au matin sur la meme chaîne. Il refuse de se resoudre a un second tour entre Marine Le Pen et Jean-Luc Melenchon, qu'il juge catastrophique pour le pays. « a la fin, cette primaire aura lieu : je crois que c'est ineluctable », a-t-il declare, soulignant qu'« aucun candidat, y compris edouard Philippe, n'est en situation d'etre au deuxieme tour » Au mois de février, chacun prendra ses responsabilités. J’ai l’habitude de prendre les miennes. En attendant, je continue d’aller à la rencontre des Français pour les écouter et leur dire ce que je propose. https://t.co/yAN9HNvEsH — Edouard Philippe (@EPhilippe_LH) November 1, 2026 Selon lui, « la division, ce n'est pas la primaire, c'est d'arriver a cinq au premier tour ». Les sondages illustrent la pression qui pese sur les heritiers d'Emmanuel Macron. edouard Philippe, encore en tete du bloc central, decroche depuis des semaines et se retrouve derriere Jean-Luc Melenchon, au coude-a-coude avec Raphael Glucksmann, loin de Marine Le Pen. Gabriel Attal, lui, est completement distance . La dispersion des candidatures (edouard Philippe, Gabriel Attal, Bruno Retailleau, David Lisnard) fait craindre une elimination collective des le premier tour. Dans ce contexte, les soutiens a une primaire se multiplient : Michel Barnier, Aurore Berge, Valerie Pecresse et David Lisnard y sont favorables tout comme Francois Bayrou, qui prone depuis plusieurs mois une grande primaire du « fleuve democratique » face a LFI et au RN . Bruno Retailleau n'y est pas oppose sous conditions de perimetre. a l'inverse, Raphael Glucksmann a rejete l'idee, y voyant « la primaire de ceux qui assument le bilan du macronisme ».

items.title: Four rooms, one country: How Ghana’s missions in New York, Geneva, The Hague and Brussels turn principle into leverage
items.description: I write as a Pan-Africanist, but I have learned to distrust slogans about African agency that never reach the rooms where agency is actually exercised. Those rooms are not summits or communiqués. They are committee chambers in New York, negotiating tables in Geneva, courtrooms and councils in The Hague, and regulatory working parties in Brussels. In each, a small team of Ghanaian diplomats sits behind a nameplate, and their work decides whether Ghana’s principles become anything more than speeches. Ghana has rarely had a better run of principle in these places. On March 25, the UN General Assembly adopted a Ghana-led resolution recognising the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans and racialised chattel enslavement as the gravest crime against humanity, and calling for reparations. The vote was 123 in favour and three against, including the United States and Israel, with 52 abstentions that included European states and the United Kingdom. In October 2026, Ghana was re-elected to the Human Rights Council for 2027 to 2029, securing 173 votes from 181 valid ballots. Applause is not a strategy, though. This article asks what Ghana’s four missions are for, what each is being asked to deliver, and where the distance lies between a won vote and a changed outcome. Four rooms, four currencies Think of the four posts as rooms that trade in different currencies. New York trades in legitimacy, because the General Assembly is where the number of states backing a position can be counted and cited. Geneva trades in credibility and technical craft, because the Human Rights Council and the trade, health and labour bodies there turn principles into rules and reviews. The Hague trades in law, because it hosts the International Court of Justice, the International Criminal Court and the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons. Brussels trades in market access, because the European Union writes regulations that Ghanaian exporters must meet whether or not Ghana had a say in the drafting. The common mistake is to treat these as four separate jobs. A mandate that wins in one room and is ignored in the others is only a quarter won. New York: where numbers become legitimacy The reparations resolution shows both the power and the limit of the General Assembly. It is not legally binding, but it carries political weight, and it gives every advocate of reparative justice a citation they did not have before. Yet the same vote shows who still needs persuading. Three states opposed it and 52 abstained, and several of those are the very governments whose cooperation any reparative framework would need. Reuters reported that supporters see the resolution as a possible path to a reparative framework and, eventually, a special tribunal. The New York mission’s task now is to turn a declaration into a process, which means patient drafting, follow-up resolutions and quiet work with the abstainers rather than further celebration. The second New York mandate is less glamorous and arguably more consequential for ordinary Ghanaians. Ghana is consistently ranked among the top ten troop-contributing countries to UN peacekeeping, with more than 2,600 personnel serving as of early 2025. Peacekeeping is paid for in the Fifth Committee, the budget body, and the UN’s liquidity crisis lands hardest on contributors. The Secretary-General has told that committee that the financial situation prevents the organisation from reimbursing troop- and police-contributing countries predictably and on time. The President has said the military high command is reviewing Ghana’s position for a post-UN-peacekeeping environment, with the possible closure of the UN force in Lebanon by the end of 2026 adding urgency. In its own contribution to the UN’s review of peace operations, Ghana argued that troop contributors should be involved in planning, and that accountability for misconduct should not stigmatise the countries that supply the troops. Those are budget and procedure arguments before they are political ones, and they need negotiators who can read a financing table as fluently as a Security Council text. Geneva: where credibility is built over years Re-election is a vote of confidence and a loan against future conduct. Under the General Assembly resolution that created the Council, members are expected to uphold the highest standards in promoting and protecting human rights and to cooperate fully with it. A member is therefore judged twice, once for what it says about others and once at its own Universal Periodic Review. Ghana should expect hard questions on its domestic record, including on matters where national debate remains unsettled, and the Geneva mission can only be as credible as Accra’s follow-through allows. Geneva’s strength is that the files meet. The same delegates handle human rights, trade, health and labour, and the mission is accredited to the UN Office, the World Trade Organisation and other international organisations there. The President has asked the incoming Permanent Representative to advance the Accra Reset agenda, which pushes for reform of global health governance, local vaccine and pharmaceutical production, and fairer access to essential health products. That is a health argument, but it is also a trade argument, since local manufacturing depends on the rules that govern technology, procurement and market entry. A delegation that sees the link can bargain across committees. One that treats each file as a silo will be outmanoeuvred by those who do not. The Hague: where law outlasts politics Ghana’s embassy in The Hague carries an unusually heavy load. Its ambassador is also Ghana’s representative to the OPCW, the ICC and the ICJ, alongside the bilateral relationship with the Netherlands. That is chemical disarmament, international criminal justice and the world’s principal court under one roof. The ICC file has a domestic side too, since Ghanaian parliamentarians visited The Hague in July 2024 to discuss draft legislation to implement the Rome Statute. The OPCW episode is instructive. Ghana nominated a career diplomat for Director-General in April 2025 and withdrew the candidacy by note verbale on 16 September 2025. In early October, the Executive Council recommended a single candidate by consensus, and the Conference of the States Parties appointed her on 27 November. I do not conclude why Ghana withdrew, because the public record does not say. The general lesson is that candidacies for international office are won in capitals and corridors well before a vote, and that a graceful exit preserves capital for the next attempt. Ghana’s national statement to the Executive Council in 2026 also recorded a mentorship partnership between its environment ministry and a UK counterpart, a reminder that technical relevance in this organisation is built through capacity as much as ambition. The Hague also holds the legal route for the reparations agenda. The UN Charter allows the General Assembly to request an advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice. Such an opinion is not binding, but it is authoritative, and it forces states to argue on legal ground rather than rhetorical ground. The obstacle every legal route must face is intertemporal law, the question of whether conduct can be judged by legal standards that did not exist when it occurred. I do not predict how the Court would answer. My point is narrower. If reparations are to move from moral claim to legal argument, the preparation will happen among lawyers who know the Court’s procedure, and Ghana’s embassy is where that knowledge has to sit. It also helps that, as Reuters noted, the Netherlands remains the only European country to have issued a formal apology for its role in slavery, so the host capital is where the European conversation is furthest advanced. Brussels: where rules are written before they reach Accra The EU Deforestation Regulation begins to apply on 30 December 2026. It requires importers of commodities such as cocoa to show that their supply chains are traceable, deforestation-free and legally produced. Implementation has already been delayed once, and the Commission published simplification measures in May 2026. The stakes are plain. More than half of Africa’s cocoa exports go to the EU, and Ghana is the world’s second largest producer. At the 2026 Ghana-EU Partnership Dialogue, the chief executive of the Ghana Investment Promotion Centre raised the problem of frequent changes in EU regulations, which is exactly the problem a Brussels mission exists to manage. A regulation is cheapest to influence while it is still a draft, so the mission must be present at the consultation stage, not the compliance stage. The political context is more complicated than the trade context. At that same dialogue in June 2026, the President called for a new phase of relations built on trade, investment, innovation and industrialisation rather than traditional aid. The EU, for its part, offered Global Gateway support for infrastructure and industry and said it was ready to engage Ghana on reparatory justice. That readiness sits awkwardly beside the abstentions in New York, and Brussels is where the difference between a polite offer and a real position can be tested. A mission that can connect an investment conversation to a reparations conversation, without letting either be held hostage to the other, would be doing real diplomatic work. What the missions need Three things follow, argued from the logic of the work rather than from anyone else’s model. First, one brief for four rooms. The President told the latest envoys that they serve in different settings but represent one country and one government, and must work within its policy framework. That principle needs machinery behind it. If the argument on historical justice in New York is not the argument in The Hague and Brussels, opponents will exploit the gap. Second, depth over churn. Reading a peacekeeping budget, drafting a legal opinion, and tracking a regulatory timetable are specialist skills that take years to build. Missions should hold researchers and specialists whose knowledge persists beyond any single posting. Third, measure what changes rather than what is said. The Foreign Ministry has designed performance indicators for ambassadors, and the President has said their work has shifted from diplomacy and protocol toward Ghana’s economic interests. That is a reasonable direction, but investment pledges are only one measure. Better indicators would include amendments secured in drafts, reimbursements recovered for troop contributors, and compliance costs avoided for exporters. What can be counted tends to be what gets done. Ghana has shown that a mid-sized African state can win the argument. Whether small and middle powers can convert that standing into material outcomes is one of the central questions in the study of the Global South, and Ghana’s four missions are a live test of it. It is the question I intend to pursue in doctoral research, and it is the one Ghana’s diplomats are answering, one drafted paragraph at a time. Dominic Senayah is an International Relations professional and policy analyst based in England, specialising in African political economy, humanitarian governance, and migration diplomacy. He holds an MA in International Relations from the UK and writes on trade policy, institutional reform, and Ghana–UK relations for audiences across Africa, the United Kingdom, and the wider Global South.

items.title: Wizz Air flight from Luton in emergency landing after bomb threat
items.description: A Wizz Air flight travelling from London Luton Airport to Sofia has been escorted by a Hungarian fighter jet to Budapest after a mid-air bomb threat. The aircraft was forced to make an emergency landing at Budapest Liszt Ferenc International. Authorities there “carried out the necessary security checks on the aircraft and passengers”, a spokesperson for Wizz Air said. The airline later confirmed an inspection had been “completed and nothing was found”, adding that the plane would depart again shortly. Hungarian Defence Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendis confirmed his country provided the fighter jet to escort the flight. According to flight tracking website FlightAware, Wizz Air flight 4302 departed Luton at 08:33 GMT and was due to arrive in the Bulgarian capital at 13:25 local time (11:25 GMT). But the website said it landed in Budapest at 12:09 local time (11:09 GMT). In a post on social media, Ruszin-Szendis said that after receiving the bomb threat, the Wizz Air flight had requested permission to land at the airport in Budapest. “Within minutes, a Hungarian Defence Forces Gripen fighter jet took to the skies and provided an escort for the passenger aircraft”, he said. After this, the jet returned to its base and police took charge of the incident, he added. The airline said that after the plane made the emergency landing, it taxied “to a designated stand” where the security checks were carried out. Wizz Air added that it was “cooperating fully with the authorities”, and that the safety of passengers and crew “remains our highest priority”.

items.title: Government convenes MMDCEs to strengthen fight against illegal mining
items.description: The government has called on Metropolitan, Municipal and District Chief Executives (MMDCEs) to take a more active role in the fight against illegal small-scale mining, warning that the destruction of water bodies, forest reserves and other natural resources requires coordinated action at all levels of governance. The call was made at the maiden National Conference of MMDCEs on Illegal Small-Scale Mining, held in Kumasi in the Ashanti Region on Monday, November 2, 2026. The conference brought together local government leaders and other stakeholders to discuss strategies for strengthening the fight against illegal mining, particularly through improved coordination between district assemblies, regulatory institutions and security agencies. The Ashanti Region, where mining activities contribute significantly to the local and regional economy and provide livelihoods for many residents, hosted the conference. Ashanti Regional Minister calls for stronger local coordination In his welcome address, the Ashanti Regional Minister, Dr Frank Amoakohene, described the conference as timely, saying it provided an important platform for stakeholders to discuss the challenges associated with illegal mining and the need for a coordinated response. He stressed that the fight against illegal mining could not be left to local authorities alone. “The fight against illegal mining cannot be left at the local level,” he said. Dr Amoakohene commended the administration of President John Dramani Mahama for what he described as its courage and political commitment to tackling the menace. “The political will of this government in the fight against illegal mining is not in doubt,” he stated. He, however, cautioned against security operations being conducted in districts without the knowledge of the respective MMDCEs, arguing that local authorities needed to be adequately informed and involved. He consequently called for appropriate communication channels and contact arrangements to be made available to MMDCEs to facilitate coordination and support for anti-illegal-mining operations. Lands Minister urges MMDCEs to take collective responsibility The Minister for Lands and Natural Resources, Emmanuel Armah-Kofi Buah, said the environmental damage caused by illegal mining over the years had made it imperative for all stakeholders, particularly local government authorities, to take collective responsibility for addressing the problem. He described mining as an important component of Ghana’s national economy but warned that the sector could not be discussed without acknowledging the environmental, economic and governance challenges associated with illegal operations. “The meeting is therefore not merely an administrative gathering, but a call to collective responsibility and decisive action,” he said. Mr Armah-Kofi Buah noted that Regional Ministers and MMDCEs occupied strategic positions in the country’s governance structure and had an important role to play in the fight. “The fight against illegal mining cannot be won by the Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources or security agencies alone. It requires our leadership, commitment, courage and sustained engagement with the people we serve,” he stressed. He described illegal mining as a serious national security concern because of its consequences for the environment, public health, food security, water resources and local economies. He said the effectiveness of the government’s response would ultimately be judged by the consistency and fairness with which leaders implemented measures to protect the country’s natural resources. “Our leadership, our government will be judged not by the statements we make at public meetings, but by the consistency, courage and fairness with which we act as leaders. We cannot pursue development today at the expense of the survival of our natural resources and communities tomorrow,” he said. The Minister identified the National Anti-Illegal Mining Operations Secretariat (NAIMOS), the Ghana Police Service, the Ghana Armed Forces and other authorised security institutions as important partners in enforcement efforts. He, however, emphasised that security operations must be complemented by effective local governance. “When NAIMOS conducts operations in a district, the Assembly must be prepared to assist with local information, logistical coordination within its lawful capacity, community engagement and follow-up monitoring,” he explained. He urged the assemblies to facilitate engagement between prospective miners and the appropriate regulatory institutions to help those interested in mining understand the procedures for obtaining the necessary authorisations. He also called on MMDCEs to communicate opportunities and requirements under approved arrangements, including cooperative mining, to interested communities. “Our goal is a mining industry that creates jobs, supports communities and safeguards our natural heritage,” he said. Assemblies urged to prioritise reclamation Mr Armah-Kofi Buah also urged MMDCEs to pay attention to the restoration of lands and water bodies already damaged by illegal mining. He warned that abandoned mining pits posed serious risks to children, farmers, livestock and other members of affected communities. He called for the promotion of tree planting, soil stabilisation, riverbank restoration and the safe treatment of abandoned mining sites in accordance with approved technical standards. “Reclamation must be treated as an essential component of environmental governance,” he stressed. To improve coordination at the local level, the Minister proposed that every mining-affected assembly establish or strengthen a district-level anti-illegal-mining coordination mechanism involving relevant decentralised departments, regulatory institutions, security agencies and community representatives. He said the government remained committed to confronting illegal mining, strengthening responsible mining practices through reforms in the sector and protecting the environment for sustainable national development. He urged the MMDCEs to recognise the long-term consequences of their decisions, saying the protection of rivers, forests and other natural resources was a responsibility to future generations. Local Government Minister warns against compromise The Minister for Local Government, Chieftaincy and Religious Affairs, Mahama Ayariga, also reiterated the government’s position against mining in water bodies. He said the practice would not be tolerated under President John Dramani Mahama’s administration. “Mining in water bodies will never be countenanced by this administration. That is a no-go area,” he declared. Mr Ayariga told participants that the conference was an opportunity for all stakeholders to examine their respective roles in addressing illegal mining. “This meeting is for all of us, who are either part of the problem or part of the solution,” he said. He also warned MMDCEs against compromising their responsibilities in the fight, stressing that public office came with accountability. “I don’t take things lightly,” he said, adding that “power and responsibility come with accountability”. He further expressed confidence in the government’s efforts to address the menace, urging the MMDCEs to support the enforcement drive. Environment Minister reiterates government’s position The Minister for Environment, Science and Technology, Dr Zanetor Agyemang-Rawlings, also reiterated the government’s position on environmental protection, stressing the importance of safeguarding the country’s natural resources. Her remarks formed part of the broader discussions at the conference on the need for coordinated action to address illegal mining and its impact on the environment.

items.title: We need committed partners willing to build with us – Victor Smith
items.description: Ghana’s Ambassador to the United States, Washington, D.C., Ambassador Victor Emmanuel Smith, has called on American investors and the Ghanaian diaspora in Tennessee to become willing partners to help build alongside the many changes and developments which are ongoing in Ghana under President John Mahama, for shared prosperity. In defining his concept of shared prosperity, the Ambassador explained that the most enduring partnerships are those in which both partners succeed. Where investors earn competitive returns, and Ghana gains industrial capacity, technology, exports, skills, and sustainable employment. He emphasized that Africa is the next great economic frontier and Ghana is ready to be a gateway to that future. Therefore, the friendship between Ghana and the United States serves as a strong foundation on which to build. He pointed out that it was time to move from conversation to collaboration, from opportunity to enterprise, and from enterprise to jobs and prosperity. “Ghana is open for business. Come, invest, build and grow with us,” he reiterated. The Ambassador was addressing the Ghana–Tennessee Business & Investor Roundtable on Thursday, October 29, which brought together Tennessee business leaders, investors, and institutional stakeholders for a structured dialogue on investment opportunities in Ghana. Accompanying the Ambassador were the Board Chair of the Ghana Medical Trust Fund, Mrs. Adjoa Obuobia Darko-Opoku, and Mr. Michael Yamson, Administrator of the District Assemblies Common Fund (DACF). Mrs. Obuobia Darko-Opoku mentioned that the areas of operation where the Ghana Medical Trust Fund would need partners were the retooling of specialist hospitals, training health professionals, research into non-communicable diseases, and partnerships with pharmaceutical companies willing to set up manufacturing plants in Ghana to augment what already exists. Mr. Yamson said the DACF has a constitutional mandate of disbursing at least 5% of national revenue for local development. He said the need is to bring industry-specific partnerships into local economic development in the areas of agriculture under the Ghana Agro Fund, climate resilience adaptation and mitigation involving waste-to-energy, carbon credits, and the grants to commerce programme, where the grant source actually benefits from their investment. The visit represents a significant opportunity to advance Ghana’s trade, agribusiness, and investment interests within one of the United States’ most dynamic and strategically positioned economies. Tennessee is home to a robust agricultural sector, a rapidly growing advanced manufacturing base, and a business climate that has consistently ranked among the most competitive in the nation. The state has proximity to major distribution corridors and established networks across the food, logistics, and technology industries. The meeting was hosted by Spencer Fane LLP and facilitated in partnership with the Ghana Investment Promotion Authority, the Nashville Black Chamber of Commerce, and the Conscious Group led by Dr. Isaac Adae. The session was designed to produce actionable outcomes for cross-border commerce and partnership.

items.title: Ogun 2027: Adebutu dismisses exclusion from INEC list
items.description: ……receives over 1,000 APC defectors into PDP in Ogun By James Ogunnaike, Abeokuta The Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) governorship candidate in Ogun State, Hon. Oladipupo Adebutu, has dismissed the omission of his name from the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) list of governorship candidates as a temporary distraction, insisting that the development would not derail his ambition to contest the 2027 governorship election. Adebutu spoke on Monday while receiving more than 1,000 defectors from the All Progressives Congress (APC) into the PDP at the party’s State Secretariat in Abeokuta, the Ogun State capital. The defectors, led by a former member of the House of Representatives, Hon. Segun William, were received by Adebutu alongside prominent PDP leaders, including the party’s Ogun Central senatorial candidate, Iyabo Obasanjo. Addressing the gathering, Adebutu expressed confidence that the controversy surrounding his omission from INEC’s list would eventually be resolved, maintaining that he remained a bona fide member of the PDP. He argued that his political history and participation in elections under the party’s platform over the past two decades were sufficient evidence of his loyalty, challenging those questioning his membership to produce evidence of when he allegedly defected. “I have been the candidate of the PDP for the last 20 years, in every election cycle. My question is: at what stage did I leave or vacate the party? Where is the proof that, for one day, I have even visited the APC office, let alone joined the party?” he asked. The PDP chieftain further disclosed that he played an active role in organising and financing the party’s recent membership registration exercise in Ogun State, which, according to him, recorded more than 19,800 members. He said his registration number in the exercise was 1536, describing the development as further evidence of his continued membership of the opposition party. Adebutu alleged that the controversy surrounding his name on the INEC list was an attempt to distract the opposition and disenfranchise voters, but assured party supporters that the PDP would remain focused on its political activities. “The controversy surrounding my name on the INEC list is an attempt to distract the opposition and disenfranchise voters. But I assure our supporters that this party will not lose focus,” he said. He also disclosed that the party had intensified its grassroots mobilisation across the state, revealing that its campaign team had visited 12 of Ogun State’s 20 local government areas and more than 140 of the 236 wards. According to him, the mobilisation exercise would continue despite what he described as efforts to distract the party from its political objectives. “We have visited 12 of the 20 local governments. Of the 236 wards, we have visited over 140. Tomorrow, we continue again because we know that the trick is to get us distracted. We will not be distracted. We will keep our eyes on the ball, and we shall win,” Adebutu declared. Earlier, William, who led the defectors, said their decision to abandon the APC and join the PDP was informed by their dissatisfaction with the ruling party’s approach to governance and what he described as its failure to uphold democratic principles and deliver genuine development to Ogun State. Recounting his political journey, William said he ventured into partisan politics in 2007, noting that although friends and associates had advised him to join the PDP at the time, he eventually aligned with the APC. He, however, said his experience in the ruling party had convinced him that the platform no longer represented the democratic ideals and developmental aspirations he believed in. William maintained that the defectors were determined to contribute to the political and socio-economic development of Ogun State through the PDP, expressing confidence in the party’s leadership. He described the APC as no longer capable of accommodating the democratic aspirations of its members and the people of the state. “We are seeking the progress of our dear Ogun State. My sincere appreciation goes first and foremost to our incoming governor, who has made this occasion possible, with the assistance of our deputy governor, our senator, the directors-general, party members, the party hierarchy and the state chairman,” William said. The defection is expected to strengthen the PDP’s mobilisation efforts in Ogun State as political parties begin positioning themselves ahead of the 2027 general elections. The post Ogun 2027: Adebutu dismisses exclusion from INEC list appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Léon XIV en Amérique latine : héritages pontificaux, recompositions du catholicisme et enjeux géopolitiques
items.description: À télécharger Lire la note (PDF) Du 6 au 17 novembre 2026, le pape Léon XIV effectuera un voyage en Uruguay, en Argentine et au Pérou, premier grand déplacement latino-américain d'un pontife dont la trajectoire personnelle est profondément liée à cette région du monde, mais dont l'élection, en mai 2025, avait également constitué une nouveauté dans l'histoire de la papauté puisque, pour la première fois, un religieux né aux États-Unis et ayant longtemps exercé son ministère au Pérou accédait au siège de Pierre. Ce déplacement présente plusieurs caractéristiques qui dépassent son importance pastorale immédiate, tant il intervient à un moment de recomposition du paysage religieux latino-américain, de transformation des rapports entre les Églises et les États, mais également d'interrogations sur l'orientation d'un pontificat dont les premières interventions ont confirmé plusieurs héritages de François sans que soit encore complètement précisée la manière dont Léon XIV entend inscrire ces orientations dans le gouvernement de l'Église universelle. L'analyse du voyage de Léon XIV suppose donc de le replacer dans cette histoire longue, en revenant sur les orientations successivement données à la présence pontificale par Jean-Paul II, Benoît XVI et François, avant d'examiner les enjeux propres à son déplacement et les contextes politiques et religieux des trois pays visités, dont les différences sont suffisamment importantes pour permettre d'observer plusieurs modalités contemporaines de relations entre catholicisme, démocratie et pouvoir politique. L’article Léon XIV en Amérique latine : héritages pontificaux, recompositions du catholicisme et enjeux géopolitiques est apparu en premier sur IRIS .

items.title: Bas-mono : La fête traditionnelle « Awatsezan », édition 2027 lancée à Afagnagan
items.description: Afagnagan, 2 nov. (ATOP) – Les manifestations de la célébration de la fête traditionnelle, historique et identitaire du peuple de Bas-Mono « Awatsèzan » édition 2027, ont été lancées, le samedi 31 octobre à Afagnagan, chef-lieu de la commune Bas-Mono 1. Cette manifestation s’inscrit dans la dynamique de la valorisation du patrimoine culturel ancestral de Bas-Mono. L’objectif est de susciter l’adhésion de la population autour de cette fête. Il s’agit pour le comité d’organisation d’expliquer le caractère endogène de la fête, son impact social et culturel et les nouvelles innovations inscrites au programme. La rencontre a permis au comité d’organisation d’informer le public sur les différentes activités culturelles, artistiques, éducatives, sportives et des jeux ludiques en disparition retenues tout au long de l’évènement. Les festivités sont placées sous le thème « De la mémoire de nos ancêtres à l’unité de notre génération d’aujourd’hui et de demain ». L’apothéose se déroulera le 27 février 2027 à Afagnagan. Ce thème met en exergue l’unité des fils et filles de la préfecture et l’importance que revêt cette célébration pour la population. L’élection Miss Awatsè va constituer l’un des temps forts de cette célébration et l’innovation de cette édition. Il aura également un tournoi de football, des jeux en disparition comme « vétrétré » et « ampé », la marche des personnes âgées, le festival des groupes folkloriques et autres activités en faveur de la population. Toutes ces activités prévues ont pour finalité de renforcer la cohésion sociale, le vivre ensemble, l’unité et de promouvoir les richesses culturelles de la préfecture. Le 1 er adjoint au maire, Dansou Romain s’est félicité de la pertinence du thème retenu pour cette célébration. Il a appelé la population à l’union et à la solidarité et invité le comité d’organisation à faire une large diffusion et sensibilisation au tour du thème. « Notre identité, c’est Awatsè. Il nous protège et nous sauve des situations difficiles » a indiqué M. Dansou. Les membres du comité d’organisation ont lancé un appel aux populations pour une mobilisation massive et leur contribution pour la promotion de la sauvegarde du patrimoine culturel et ancestral. Ils ont invité à œuvrer pour que cette édition se fasse dans une ambiance de ferveur et de communion. L’évènement a été marqué par une cérémonie de libation, le tout dans une ambiance entretenue par un groupe folklorique et du tam-tam parlant. La cérémonie a mobilisé des autorités locales, des chefs traditionnels, des responsables des services déconcentrés de l’Etat et des populations. ATOP/DK/SED/KYA

items.title: CNSS : Les acteurs de la chaîne financière et comptable à l'école du régime fiscal
items.description: La Caisse nationale de sécurité sociale (CNSS) a entamé, ce lundi 2 novembre 2026 à Koudougou, un atelier de formation de cinq jours au profit des acteurs de sa chaîne financière et comptable. Cette session vise à renforcer leurs compétences sur le régime fiscal applicable à l'institution. Dans un contexte marqué par l'évolution constante de la législation fiscale, la maîtrise des obligations fiscales constitue un enjeu majeur pour la bonne gouvernance et la performance de la Caisse nationale de sécurité sociale (CNSS). C'est dans cette perspective que la direction générale de l'institution a initié un atelier de formation de cinq jours à Koudougou au profit des cadres et agents intervenant dans la chaîne financière et comptable. Prévu du 2 au 6 novembre 2026, cet atelier permettra aux participants d'approfondir leurs connaissances sur le régime fiscal applicable à la CNSS, notamment en matière d'obligations déclaratives et de paiement. Au cours de la formation, les acteurs aborderont des modules tels que la généralité, la facturation au Burkina Faso, la retenue à la source, la fiscalité immobilière et le processus de sécurisation des terres au Burkina. Quelques employés de la CNSS à l'atelier de formation. Les travaux devront également contribuer à une meilleure appropriation des textes en vigueur, à l'harmonisation des pratiques, à l'identification des principales zones de risque ainsi qu'au renforcement des mécanismes internes de contrôle et de suivi. Au nom du directeur général de la CNSS, le secrétaire général, Léopold Toé, a souligné que cette formation vise à renforcer la compréhension du régime fiscal applicable à l'institution. Elle devra ainsi permettre aux différents acteurs de mieux cerner les incidences fiscales de leurs activités et d'améliorer la prévention des risques. Il a relevé que toute erreur d'interprétation des textes ou tout manquement aux obligations déclaratives et aux échéances de paiement est susceptible d'exposer l'institution à des redressements, des pénalités financières ou des contentieux. Pour le secrétaire général, la conformité fiscale ne doit donc pas être considérée comme une responsabilité exclusive des services spécialisés, mais comme une préoccupation partagée par tous les acteurs de la chaîne financière et comptable. Le secrétaire général de la CNSS, Léopold Toé. « La conformité fiscale ne relève donc pas uniquement des services spécialisés. Elle constitue une responsabilité partagée par l'ensemble des acteurs de la chaîne financière et comptable. Camarades, c'est pour répondre à cette exigence que la direction générale a jugé opportune d'organiser le présent atelier », a-t-il insisté, invitant les participants à prendre une part active aux communications et aux échanges. Pour Karim Nignan, conseiller fiscal auprès de la direction générale de la CNSS et par ailleurs formateur à l'atelier, cette formation s'inscrit dans la dynamique de renforcement continu des capacités des cadres et agents de l'institution. Elle répond notamment à la nécessité de permettre aux praticiens de mieux comprendre les difficultés liées à l'application de la législation fiscale, dans un environnement réglementaire en constante évolution. Karim Nignan, conseiller fiscal auprès de la direction générale de la CNSS. « Durant ces 5 jours, nous allons passer en revue le régime fiscal applicable à la Caisse nationale de sécurité sociale, les obligations déclaratives et de paiement. Nous allons voir essentiellement les différents impôts et taxes qui sont déclarés et payés par la CNSS », a-t-il indiqué. Pour le conseiller fiscal, les activités de la CNSS comportent plusieurs implications fiscales. En sa qualité d'organisme chargé de la protection sociale des travailleurs, l'institution réalise notamment des acquisitions, conclut des contrats et des marchés, et effectue des investissements dans le domaine immobilier. Autant d'opérations qui nécessitent une bonne maîtrise des dispositions fiscales applicables. Jean-Élysée Nikiéma Lefaso.net

items.title: Le président de la Chambre islamique inaugure le chapitre européen de l’initiative B57+
items.description: Istanbul, 2 nov . (ATOP) – Le président de la Chambre islamique de commerce et de développement (ICCD), M. Abdullah Saleh Kamel, a affirmé le 1 er novembre, à Istamboul, que le monde islamique dispose de capitaux, de ressources, de marchés et de compétences humaines lui permettant de devenir une puissance économique plus influente. Il a souligné que le véritable défi consiste à « transformer ces potentialités en investissements, en projets et en partenariats au service de nos intérêts communs ». Ces déclarations ont été faites lors de son allocution à l’ouverture de la deuxième édition du Sommet des dirigeants d’entreprises, organisé par la Chambre islamique de commerce et de développement sous le thème « La Grande Convergence », à Istanbul, en marge de la 42ᵉ session du Comité permanent pour la coopération économique et commerciale de l’Organisation de la coopération islamique (COMCEC), en présence du ministre turc du Commerce, M. Ömer Bolat. Ce sommet s’inscrit dans le cadre de l’initiative B57+, une initiative internationale lancée en 2025 par la Chambre islamique de commerce et de développement, sous la supervision directe du vice-président de la République de Türkiye, M. Cevdet Yılmaz. Elle rassemble les dirigeants d’entreprise des 57 États membres de l’Organisation de la coopération islamique (OCI) et leurs homologues du monde entier, dans le but de transformer le dialogue en investissements, en projets et en partenariats à impact durable. Le Sommet des dirigeants d’entreprises se tient chaque année dans le cadre de cette initiative, dont la présente édition constitue la deuxième. Une distinction M. Abdullah Saleh Kamel a inauguré le chapitre européen de l’initiative B57+, dont les premières activités débuteront à Bruxelles dans les prochaines semaines. Ce nouveau chapitre vise à établir un pont de coopération économique entre les milieux d’affaires des États membres de l’OCI et leurs homologues européens. Il a remercié l’Union des chambres et des bourses de commerce de Türkiye (TOBB), ainsi que son président, M. Rifat Hisarcıklıoğlu, pour leur soutien aux préparatifs de ce nouveau chapitre, exprimant l’espoir de voir prochainement ouvrir un bureau de l’initiative au siège de l’Union à Bruxelles. Le président de la Chambre islamique de commerce et de développement a indiqué que ce sommet intervenait à l’issue d’une semaine spécialisée dans le règlement des différends commerciaux par la médiation et l’arbitrage, à laquelle ont participé des centres issus des États membres de l’OCI ainsi que des organismes établis au Royaume-Uni, aux États-Unis et au Canada. Il a souligné que cette coopération contribue à surmonter l’un des principaux obstacles à l’investissement étranger, notamment dans les pays les moins avancés, affirmant que « la confiance dans l’environnement des affaires constitue le fondement de l’attraction des investissements ». M. Abdullah Saleh Kamel a également insisté sur le fait que la complémentarité dans les différents secteurs industriels est devenue un impératif. Il a précisé que l’intégration logistique, en garantissant la stabilité des chaînes et des voies d’approvisionnement, facilitera les échanges commerciaux et favorisera l’augmentation des exportations entre les États membres ajoutant que la réussite de toute initiative doit se mesurer à l’aune des projets, des investissements et des partenariats effectivement concrétisés sur le terrain. Le président de la Chambre a enfin exprimé l’ambition de faire de B57+ une plateforme de coopération permanente entre les dirigeants d’entreprise tout au long de l’année, « où les idées se transforment en initiatives, les initiatives en projets et les projets en retombées économiques concrètes ». L ’initiative B57+ B57+ est une initiative internationale lancée en 2025 par la Chambre islamique de commerce et de développement. Son appellation fait référence aux 57 États membres de l’Organisation de la coopération islamique et à leurs partenaires à travers le monde. Elle rassemble des dirigeants d’entreprises issus de ces pays et d’autres régions du monde afin d’examiner les enjeux économiques contemporains, d’étudier les difficultés rencontrées par les entreprises dans les domaines du commerce, de l’investissement et du financement, puis de traduire les résultats de ces échanges en initiatives et en projets économiques à impact durable. L’initiative repose sur trois plateformes complémentaires. La première est le Sommet des dirigeants d’entreprises, organisé annuellement, dont la deuxième édition s’est tenue à Istanbul en novembre 2026 sous le thème « La Grande Convergence ». La deuxième consiste en une semaine spécialisée consacrée au règlement des différends commerciaux par la médiation et l’arbitrage, avec la participation de centres issus des États membres de l’OCI, du Royaume-Uni, des États-Unis et du Canada. La troisième est le chapitre européen, dont les activités seront lancées à Bruxelles avec le soutien de l’Union des chambres et des bourses de commerce de Türkiye (TOBB). L a Chambre islamique de commerce et de développement Elle une organisation internationale non gouvernementale issue de l’Organisation de la coopération islamique. Fondée en 1977 à Istanbul, elle représente le secteur privé des États membres et œuvre au renforcement de leur coopération commerciale et économique, à la promotion des investissements conjoints, au développement des projets transfrontaliers et à l’accroissement des échanges commerciaux intra-OCI. Elle regroupe 57 États membres et son siège principal est situé à Karachi, en République islamique du Pakistan. En décembre 2023, elle a adopté sa dénomination actuelle de « Chambre islamique de commerce et de développement ». Elle est présidée par M. Abdullah Saleh Kamel. ATOP/KYA/Source UNA

items.description: C’est une fin anticipée pour l’athlète sénégalaise Woreye Ndiaye. Elle a été déclarée forfait lundi, après une blessure le dimanche lors de son premier passage en Tadjiquan Combiné, une épreuve de wushu. La compétition s’arrête prématurément pour Woreye Ndiaye. Blessée le dimanche lors de son premier passage en Tadjiquan Combiné, l’athlète sénégalaise ne pourra pas poursuivre l’aventure. Son entraîneur, Ousmane Sakho, a confirmé son forfait lundi. C'est dans cette dernière épreuve que la Sénégalaise Woreye Ndiaye s'est illustrée. « Pour moi, c'est un grand honneur de représenter mon pays et d'avoir été sur le tapis pour représenter mon pays, le Sénégal », avait-t-elle savouré après un passage accompagné par les clameurs du public. A lire aussi : JOJ Dakar 2026 : le Sénégal s’incline face à l’Australie en rugby féminin L'évènement était forcément particulier pour elle, mais aussi pour tout un pays et tout le monde du wushu. Il convient de noter qu’elle était en 10e position dans le classement des résultats du 1er tour de Taijishan femmes. Il faut noter qu’avant le tournoi, elle avait notamment suivi une préparation intensive de deux mois en Chine, à Tianjin, afin de parfaire sa technique sous la direction d'entraîneurs de haut niveau Mariama DIEME

items.title: La Finlande entame la mise en œuvre de l’initiative française de dissuasion nucléaire, selon le président Alexander Stubb
items.description: La Finlande a commence a mettre en œuvre l'initiative francaise de dissuasion nucleaire, a annonce le 2 novembre le president finlandais Alexander Stubb. Les travaux officiels ont debute la semaine precedente, a-t-il precise lors de l'ouverture du 258e cours de defense nationale, a Helsinki. Helsinki avait rejoint le projet francais en septembre. Selon Stubb, la cooperation doit permettre a la Finlande de mieux comprendre les decisions strategiques des grandes puissances et de renforcer la dissuasion collective. Le chef de l'etat a aussi evoque la diminution du role des etats-Unis dans la securite europeenne, estimant que les pays du continent devaient davantage compter sur leurs propres capacites. Pour autant, aucun cadre definitif n'a encore ete arrete. Les autorites finlandaises doivent examiner les differentes possibilites et leurs consequences avant de trancher sur l'etendue de leur participation. Un projet d'elargissement de la cooperation nucleaire europeenne Presentee en mars par le president francais Emmanuel Macron, l'initiative francaise repose sur le concept de « dissuasion avancee ». Elle prevoit notamment des exercices conjoints avec des partenaires europeens et la possibilite de deployer certains elements des forces strategiques francaises sur leur territoire. Paris a par ailleurs annonce vouloir augmenter son arsenal nucleaire et ne plus rendre public le nombre exact de ses ogives. Dix pays europeens, dont la Finlande, ont rejoint l'initiative. Leur adhesion ne leur donne toutefois aucun controle sur les armes nucleaires francaises, dont l'utilisation reste soumise aux seules decisions de Paris. Le dispositif demeure distinct de celui de l'Organisation du traite de l'Atlantique nord. La Finlande beneficie deja de la dissuasion nucleaire de l'Alliance atlantique, qu'elle a rejointe en 2023. En octobre, ses forces armees ont participe a l'exercice nucleaire annuel Steadfast Noon . Le ministre finlandais de la Defense Antti Häkkänen avait alors juge la demarche conforme aux objectifs de securite du pays. La cooperation avec Paris n'implique toutefois pas necessairement le stationnement d'armes nucleaires francaises en Finlande. La ministre finlandaise des Affaires etrangeres Elina Valtonen a precise qu'Helsinki n'envisageait pas, a ce stade, d'accueillir de telles armes sur son territoire. Moscou denonce les risques pour la stabilite strategique Les projets de renforcement nucleaire en Europe ont deja suscite des avertissements de la Russie. En mai, l'ambassadeur russe en Allemagne Sergueï Netchaïev avait declare que l'elargissement du « parapluie nucleaire » europeen constituait une menace strategique directe pour la Russie, appelant a en tenir compte dans la planification militaro-politique du pays. Moscou a en outre mis en cause les consequences de l'augmentation des capacites nucleaires occidentales pour le regime international de non-proliferation. Toujours en mai, le diplomate russe Andreï Beloussov avait accuse les etats-Unis, le Royaume-Uni et la France de renforcer leurs arsenaux sans tenir compte du Traite sur la non-proliferation des armes nucleaires.
