items.title: Consumer inflation falls to 9.6pc in Oct from 10.3pc in Sept
items.description: ISLAMABAD: Consumer inflation eased to 9.6 per cent in October from 10.3pc a month earlier , mainly due to a slight slowdown in perishable food products, the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics said on Monday. The slowdown in the inflation rate for the second consecutive month, measured by the Consumer Price Index, reversed the sharp increase recorded in August , when higher food and energy prices pushed the annual rate to 11.1pc from 9.2pc in July. The easing was recorded in both places, in rural areas where inflation fell to 9.5pc from 10.1pc, while urban inflation edged down to 9.8pc from 10.5pc. The October reading was also within the Ministry of Finance’s projection of 9.5pc to 10.5pc for the month in its Monthly Economic Update and Outlook for October . According to the finance ministry, easing headline inflation offers some relief, while improved crop supplies can help ease food price pressures. However, despite the decline in the annual rate, prices rose 1.1pc month-on-month in October. The annual inflation rate was 6.2pc in October last year. The average inflation between July and October stood at 10.05pc compared with 4.79pc over the corresponding period last year. The easing was largely driven by perishable food prices. Food inflation dropped to 7.8pc in urban areas in October from 8.1pc in September. The decline was much sharper in rural areas, where food inflation fell to 7.1pc from 7.7pc a month earlier. However, non-food inflation moved in the opposite direction, indicating continued pressure on household expenses. Urban non-food inflation decelerated to 10.6pc from 11.5pc in September, while rural non-food inflation fell to 12.3pc from 13.1pc. The latest data shows that the composition of inflation shifted in October. While food inflation slowed sharply, electricity and transport costs continued to rise. Electricity charges increased by 8.50pc from the previous month, while transport prices rose by 30.39pc in urban areas. At the national level, transport costs increased by 1.79pc during October from the previous month and were 28.61pc higher than in the same month last year. Housing, water, electricity, gas and fuels increased by 0.25pc during the month and by 11.03pc on an annual basis. Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy components, also eased slightly. It stood at 7.8pc in urban areas in October, compared with 8.6pc in September, while the rural rate declined to 7.1pc from 8.1pc.

items.description: “Toda la casa [por el gestor de la infraestructura ferroviaria Adif] está tensionada muy por encima de sus posibilidades en busca de respuestas al accidente de Urda , cuando aún no hemos salido del estado de shock , y manteniendo la operativa en la red de alta velocidad y en la convencional”. El diagnóstico de situación crítica es de un alto directivo de Adif que reclama el anonimato antes de una breve conversación. Lejos de parar máquinas para analizar lo sucedido en Urda (Toledo), el ritmo frenético diario debe continuar en los centros de control . Pero son horas decisivas para el curso de la investigación del siniestro que el pasado miércoles 28 de octubre costó la vida a 69 personas en la línea de altas prestaciones Madrid-Sevilla. El presidente de Adif, Luis Pedro Marco de la Peña, tiene toda la presión sobre los hombros, al igual que todo su comité ejecutivo. El cargo, afirman fuentes internas, está a disposición del ministro de Transportes desde el primer minuto. Y el de Óscar Puente , en manos del presidente del Gobierno. El cese de Marco de la Peña, antes o junto al de Puente, es un clamor entre los grupos de la oposición, también entre aliados del Grupo Socialista en el Congreso. Puente y Marco de la Peña, que comparecieron juntos en rueda de prensa el pasado viernes, se comprometieron en enero a trabajar para que un suceso como el de Adamuz (Córdoba), en la misma línea Madrid-Sevilla, no se repitiera . Dans une déclaration à Diwan FM , Mouna Arfaoui, la directrice de l’association organisatrice, a avancé le chiffre d’un million de visiteurs, qui nous semble cependant quelque peu exagéré. Il y a eu des points de vente directe de grenades (du producteur au consommateur), ainsi que des séminaires visant à valoriser cette richesse agricole et à faire connaître ses spécificités, a-t-elle ajouté, en faisant part de sa volonté de donner au festival une dimension internationale afin d’impulser l’activité touristique dans cette ville fondée au Moyen-Âge par les Morisques Andalous chassés d’Espagne par la Reconquista chrétienne. Rappelons de la production tunisienne de grenades est estimée à 98 000 tonnes pour la saison 2026, ce qui représente une hausse de 8 % par rapport à la saison précédente (91 000 tonnes). Ce fruit est produit dans deux régions principales: Gabès, dans le sud-est, connue pour sa variété Gapsi protégée par une AOC, et Testour, pôle historique célèbre pour son Festival des grenades et ses certifications biologiques Ecocert . items.title: The Racism Scam
items.description: Faced with flagging numbers over an unpopular and unnecessary war in Iran, inflation exacerbated by tariffs, lawless immigration enforcement, and corruption, Republicans have gone back to basics for their closing message: stoking hatred against minority groups. The Michigan Senate campaign between Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has been particularly ugly. Rogers has accused El-Sayed —without any evidence—of being “bought off by the Muslim Brotherhood.” At a recent rally, J. D. Vance said El-Sayed harbored “anti-white racial hate,” and President Trump called him a “jihadist” who would need to go through a “metal detector” to enter the Senate. The only time in recent memory that the Senate was subject to political violence, it is worth noting, is when Trump himself incited an attack on it. This kind of rhetoric has spilled over into Ohio, where Republican Senator Bernie Moreno asked at a rally whether El-Sayed knew that “Jesus came here for our salvation.” The Founding Fathers were committed to religious freedom, and embedded no religious test for public office in the Constitution. That’s actually good news for Republicans, because their nominee for governor of Ohio is Vivek Ramaswamy, who is Hindu. Republican attacks elsewhere have also focused on vulnerable minorities. Iowa Republican Ashley Hinson has accused her Democratic opponent, Josh Turek, of voting “to allow government employees to help their kids change their gender at school and keep it secret from the parents.” Anti-trans ads are a GOP staple in Texas, where Republicans backing the Senate candidate Ken Paxton have tried to turn allegations of corruption and infidelity into a positive by attacking Democrat James Talarico’s masculinity. Also in Texas, Republican Governor Greg Abbott, who’s in a close race with Democrat Gina Hinojosa, has accused his Catholic opponent of supporting “Sharia law.” On Halloween, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins posted a fake costume for a “SNAP fraudster,” complete with handcuffs and piles of “taxpayers cash,” that was little more than a racist stereotype about Black people. [ David A. Graham: Islamophobia is Trump’s closing midterm gambit ] All of this has coincided with Trump’s usual race-baiting about immigration. Pointing to unrest in France, the president posted on his social network that “the immigration of people from an entirely different world, people with hatred in their hearts, has shattered that once great country.” The idea that there was no history of violent protest in France before immigrants got there is—well, let’s say you have to know very little about France to believe that one. Still, the message is pretty clear: If you let people who aren’t white into your country, you will get riots. Trump made himself even clearer at a rally in Kansas , saying, “Dumocrats are the party of anti-Western, Marxist, and hostile Third World migrants.” Overt bigotry is nothing new for Trump or the Trump-era Republican Party. One reason the GOP is betting the House and Senate on this approach working is that the electorate has not rebuked it often or forcefully enough. Republicans didn’t draw the line when Trump called Somalis “garbage” or when he slandered Haitian immigrants as pet eaters. (When former President Barack Obama said Trump made the White House look like “Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory,” however, that was outrageous—“super elitist,” according to Vance .) Put simply, bigotry remains a large part of American politics because some American voters like it, and many others do not find it disqualifying. If Republicans thought this kind of talk was politically ineffective, they would not engage in it. [ From the June 2019 issue: An oral history of Trump’s bigotry ] MAGA has historically bet on white identity politics to mobilize white voters in large enough numbers to give Republicans an insurmountable advantage in the Senate and Electoral College. To this end, right-wing candidates have tried to make fears of minority groups as salient as possible every election cycle, even if it requires senseless conspiracy theories . In 2024, Trump won over more Black and Hispanic voters than in the past, making it seem as if the one weakness in that strategy—that nonwhite voters would be repelled by it—could be surmounted. (That year was a particular economic environment, however, and it’s possible Republicans overinterpreted those results as a more profound endorsement than they really were.) But at this point, Americans should recognize this campaign for the cynical gambit that it is. Trump’s scapegoating has not solved any problems. It has not brought down inflation or the cost of living; it has not raised wages or led to greater job growth . The only winners of the Trump administration are his family members, whose wealth has grown since he took office, and industries that have enjoyed favorable regulatory decisions or lavish tax cuts. For those at the top, bigotry provides a justification for unearned advantages—while for those at the bottom, it can serve as an explanation for life’s disappointments. One thing it can’t do, though, is provide the broad-based prosperity Trump promises. At the turn of the 19th century, the populist Tom Watson wrote that Black and white laborers were “kept apart that you may be separately fleeced of your earnings. You are made to hate each other because upon that hatred is rested the keystone of the arch of financial despotism that enslaves you both.” Tragically, Watson later abandoned this insight—he became an arch racist and anti-Semite. The bigger tragedy is that more than a century later, a major political party is still trying to make this scam work.

items.title: Does Morris Katz Know What Working-Class Voters Want?
items.description: O ne day over the summer, Morris Katz slouched into our booth at a diner in Brooklyn Heights, removed his backwards baseball cap, and stuffed a Zyn pouch into his mouth. He took out his iPhone (no case, gaping crack down the back) and put it face down on the table. Then, while claiming, “I never do this,” he plunked a Hershey’s kiss into his espresso. The 27-year-old political strategist and Zohran Mamdani confidant was ready to speak. Katz believes that the Democratic Party is beholden to billionaire oligarchs and is out of touch with the economic issues that working people care about. The world has worsened for most Americans, and he thinks Democrats are afraid to name the culprits. “You can’t tell someone they’re getting fucked and not tell them who’s fucking them,” Katz said. He loathes politicians who seek incremental change. The party, he says, needs to run outsiders who promise to blow up a corrupt system. Katz is articulate (profane, but articulate), confident, and podcast-ready. When it comes to his day job, making campaign ads, even Katz’s critics concede that he is a generational talent. He made his name on Mamdani’s New York City mayoral campaign. David Axelrod became a mentor. Other campaigns across the country couldn’t wait to hire him. He was on a vertical trajectory through much of 2026. One of his biggest victories came in June, when his client Graham Platner defeated Maine Governor Janet Mills in the state’s Senate primary. Then everything imploded. Platner dropped out of the race following a cornucopia of scandals, involving everything from Nazi tattoos to rape allegations. Katz was ridiculed, and Democrats seemed to recognize the risk they’d taken in entrusting a crucial Senate race to someone too young to remember September 11. But Katz remains a force in Democratic politics heading into the midterms. Fight Agency, the firm where Katz is a partner, was set up to support progressive outsiders running for office. Katz seeks out candidates who can be credible populist messengers. Whether they are in fact members of the working class—Platner relied on money from his wealthy parents well into adulthood—matters less to him than whether they come across that way. They need to look the part: beards, Carhartt, and tattoos (except Nazi ones) are a plus. And they must be charismatic public speakers, both in front of a crowd and mediated through an iPhone. The ads that Katz makes aren’t subtle. Recent spots for Brian Poindexter, an ironworker running for Congress in Ohio, feature the candidate playing football, driving a forklift, and promising that he wants to “go build stuff,” not think about politics. Other Katz clients weld, farm, and fix heavy machinery on-screen. Katz, it should be said, does not weld, farm, or fix heavy machinery. He is a child of urban privilege. More on that in a minute. Pointedly missing from Katz’s vision is the idea that Democrats need to move to the center on social issues. Katz believes that if Democrats fully embrace confrontational economic populism, they will make cultural moderation unnecessary, because voters care more about material concerns. A class war, in other words, will trump the culture war. In one recent Katz-produced ad, Gina Hinojosa, running to unseat Governor Greg Abbott in Texas, tells the camera , “They want to run an entire campaign saying that I’m too woke. Let’s roll. I plan to spend an entire campaign focused on the fact that working people are too broke.” Katz’s clients have been successful in intra-party contests in some deep-blue areas, including New York City. One Katz candidate and Mamdani ally, Claire Valdez, is a former Columbia University union worker who supports abolishing ICE and promises to invest in “queer and trans liberation.” She defeated the handpicked successor of the retiring incumbent in her primary this summer, and is the overwhelming favorite to win the general election. She’ll be representing parts of northern Brooklyn and western Queens in Congress come January. Winning over voters outside Brooklyn and Brooklyn-like regions is another story. Fight Agency’s candidates have so far struggled in purple states.They perform best with a growing cohort of young, highly educated, downwardly mobile voters—not coincidentally, the kind of voters most likely to hold progressive views on both economic and cultural issues. Katz’s candidates correctly sense that people want representatives who will fight against the establishment, Axelrod told me. “But progressive politicians and their supporters, consultants, and strategists have to recognize that it’s hard to lead a working-class movement if the working class isn’t following,” he said. Katz believes that he will be vindicated. And he has held on to a surprising amount of power following the Platner fiasco. He is working for something like 12 candidates and two super PACs (he told me he’d have his assistant follow up with the exact numbers because he couldn’t remember them; she said it changes so often that she can’t provide a full list), while informally helping Abdul El-Sayed’s Senate campaign in Michigan. Katz, or at least Katzism, could determine whether Democrats win or lose in the midterms. The question of whether Katz has unlocked a formula for winning back working-class voters, or is instead speaking to the disenchanted sons and daughters of the upper-middle class—people like him—has therefore become a matter of national importance. L ike many professional economic populists, Katz comes from a privileged background. His grandfather Harry Jay Katz was heir to a hosiery fortune and an infamous Philadelphia playboy. His mother is a successful children’s-book author; his father is a screenwriter and producer whose credits include the John Leguizamo comedy The Pest . As a kid growing up in Tribeca—an actual working-class neighborhood, a very long time ago—Katz thought he would write plays or films himself one day. Much of his political education seems to have come from movies. A favorite is Angels With Dirty Faces , about the divergent paths of two boys who attempt to rob a train car. One evades the police and later becomes a priest; the other is caught, embarks on a life of crime, and is executed by the state. Katz quoted the last line to me: “All right, fellas, let’s go and say a prayer for a boy who couldn’t run as fast as I could.” The moral of the film, he said, was that “there is a randomness to who gets to succeed and who doesn’t.” Other political lessons came on the job. During the pandemic, he dropped out of Skidmore College to manage Erica Smith’s campaign for a North Carolina congressional seat. Katz, who was 21 at the time, cast himself in the role of experienced political operator, telling people he was 23 to seem more credible. He met Rebecca Katz (no relation), who would later hire him at Fight Agency. In hindsight, they laugh about how clueless he was. But to others, he appeared preternaturally self-assured. When the Democratic strategist Adam Jentleson called him to offer advice and assistance, Katz instead lectured him on how to court working-class voters. Jentleson was aghast. “There’s nothing in his background that struck me as offering him any additional insight into how to win working-class people,” Jentleson told me. “It was like, Why should I listen to this kid? ” (The relationship between Katz and Jentleson, whose consulting firm caters to more moderate candidates, has only deteriorated since then. Katz said that the story was “fabricated,” and that he had asked Jentleson for advice and explained his campaign plan.) [ Jonathan Chait: The crisis for Democrats in Michigan ] Katz accompanied Smith on a tour of all 100 counties in North Carolina. People in the counties that went for Trump had the same problems as reliably blue voters, Katz realized. But they didn’t want to hear about the Green New Deal or any other progressive hobbyhorses. Over time, he revised Smith’s stump speech to focus on her personal story instead of her policies. As the primary neared, Katz felt confident in his candidate’s chances. Then AIPAC, the pro-Israel lobbying group, spent more than $2 million attacking Smith and boosting her primary-election opponent. Smith ended up losing. Katz insists that if AIPAC hadn’t gotten involved, she would have won. He became convinced that elites were distorting democracy by thwarting the will of the people. He brought this belief to congressional campaigns for Pennsylvania’s John Fetterman (who won), New York’s Jamaal Bowman (who lost), and Nebraska’s Dan Osborn (who lost in 2024 and is running again). But he would probably still be merely another young ad maker if not for Zohran Mamdani. I n 2024, Mamdani—then a barely known state-assembly member—asked Katz to coffee. Within two minutes, Katz thought Mamdani could be the next mayor. He helped create Mamdani’s launch video, in which the young candidate dedicated his campaign to working-class New Yorkers and promised, “We can afford to dream.” From the start, Katz was unlike other members of the team. Staffers often rope family and friends into appearing as extras in campaign ads. For Mamdani’s first television commercial, when an extra dropped out at the last minute, Katz found a replacement in Mimi O’Donnell, the longtime girlfriend of the late actor Philip Seymour Hoffman—Katz’s godfather. Katz took colleagues out for steak dinners with seafood towers and martinis, sometimes expensing the bill and sometimes paying himself, one told me. The waiters always recognized him. Mamdani’s campaign became famous for its use of direct-to-camera video to connect with voters. When the candidate entered the race, he was polling in the single digits. But he flooded social media with clips that appeared spontaneous and relatable, helping them go viral. In one, he talked about how inflation had increased the cost of street-cart chicken. In July 2025, he won the primary by 12 points. Katz got much of the credit. One profile of the strategist, published in Vanity Fair , praised him for “helping engineer Mamdani’s rise.” He’s been called a “wunderkind” more times than he can count. In fact, Katz didn’t make any of the viral social-media videos. He advised on communication strategy, but stepped in to make Mamdani’s television ads only once the candidate had the funding and name recognition to pay for them. Fate had also helped Mamdani hugely by giving him a pathologically flawed opponent, former New York Governor Andrew Cuomo. The wunderkind narrative therefore rankles some of his former colleagues. I spoke with a number of Mamdani-campaign staffers—all of whom requested anonymity to avoid jeopardizing their career—who took issue with how much credit Katz got. “Enough with this guy,” one said. The staffers seemed confused by how Katz had come to be seen as responsible for the mayor’s success. But perhaps it shouldn’t have been surprising. Katz’s day job involves portraying privileged candidates as paragons of the working class. A similar logic might explain his own trajectory: The smooth-talking consultant who claims he knows how to win over skeptical voters gets credit for it—regardless of the underlying reality. K atz thought he had his next coup with Graham Platner. Katz helped persuade him to run for Senate in Maine and helped make his launch video. The video is warm-hued, set against sun-dappled Maine-waterfront backdrops. In it, the candidate does kettlebell swings, farms oysters in a stained sweatshirt, chops wood, and declares that “the enemy is the oligarchy; it’s the billionaires who pay for it, the politicians who sell us out.” The video received more than 2.5 million views within 24 hours. But almost immediately, incriminating details emerged about Platner’s past. First came the discovery of offensive Reddit posts, then the revelation that he had a Nazi symbol tattooed on his chest. Katz was playing a leadership role but was unprepared for the responsibility, according to his former colleagues on the Platner campaign. “It felt like there were no adults in the room,” one of them told me. “He’s a decent person and quite smart, but taking on roles that he doesn’t have experience in doing.” Katz would be better off if he spent less time talking to reporters, the colleague said. (In our interviews, Katz insisted he doesn’t want media attention.) Platner ran as an insurgent challenging Governor Mills, Chuck Schumer’s preferred choice. While Mills ran as a conventional Democrat, Platner supported Medicare for All, abolishing ICE, and ending aid to Israel. Even with his vulnerabilities, he easily won the primary. Polling suggested that voters saw Platner—a tattooed, mustachioed guy with a deep voice—as relatively moderate, despite his policy positions. To Katz, those polls vindicated his theory of politics: As long as a candidate runs on economic populism and can credibly play the role of the blue-collar outsider, voters will follow. But how Platner would have fared in the general election is unknowable; after the primary, he began sliding in the polls. In July, Politico published the account of a woman who accused Platner of raping her. Platner denied the allegation. Two days later, he dropped out of the race. [ Tyler Austin Harper: The contradictions of Troy Jackson ] Katz has been severely criticized for the Platner episode. In the Los Angeles mayoral race, one candidate has been attacked for working with Katz. Hundreds of members of the Democratic Socialists of America signed a letter accusing Katz of having “appropriated the American working class’s burgeoning desire for authentic champions.” They asked that DSA-aligned politicians disavow him. The media discourse frustrates him, he told me; he never asked to be cast in the role of the Democrats’ savior. “It’s like, This guy thinks he’s such a fucking genius, and look at him now . I never said that. Like, you guys said that!” Mamdani has kept Katz on as one of his closest advisers. And Katz is already talking about how he’ll apply the lessons he learned in Maine. “Obviously I fucked up with Graham, and there are, like, a million things I would do differently now,” he said. In hindsight, he says the Reddit posts should have been the red line that forced Platner to drop out of the race. I asked Katz what that line should be in the future. “It’s a little bit like, you know it when you see it,” he said. (He had, of course, just missed a red line when he saw it.) Katz still believes in his theory of politics. After all, he said, if establishment Democrats are so smart, why do Republicans control the White House and both houses of Congress? And now he has plenty of chances to show that Katzism offers a viable alternative. Katz spends much of his time flying across the country to shoot ads for his midterm candidates. These include Randy Villegas (a Bernie Sanders–endorsed former teacher running to flip a congressional seat in California) and Donavan McKinney (a DSA member who ousted the incumbent Democrat in a safely blue Michigan congressional district). Some of the ads resemble short films more than campaign spots. A recent video for Gina Hinojosa features clips of the candidate talking about her choice to continue a pregnancy even after doctors told her the baby would not survive outside the womb—a subtle and somewhat un-Katzian gesture toward cultural moderation. (“There is room for cultural moderation in a district-specific, state-specific way,” Katz allowed when I mentioned the ad.) His influence is strongest in New York, where he works for three Mamdani-backed candidates who are all but certain to win congressional seats in November. But his candidates still have yet to prove that they can attract the working-class voters Democrats need to win back. In his Senate race, Fetterman did best in traditionally Democratic areas—college towns, urban areas, and highly educated suburbs. In working-class areas, he performed significantly worse than the moderate, suit-wearing Josh Shapiro, who won the governor’s race in a landslide. (Since his election, Fetterman has become one of the most conservative Democrats in the Senate.) Mamdani dominated in neighborhoods with a high proportion of young people, renters, and college graduates. In Bushwick and Prospect Heights, for example, he beat Cuomo by nearly 70 points, while Cuomo won in heavily working-class Staten Island. In Michigan’s primary, El-Sayed won in precincts where people had higher education levels but lower incomes. Katz seems to have an uncanny ability to speak to a population that grew up accustomed to a comfortable lifestyle and now doubt whether they’ll have what their parents did. But his efforts to reach the working class seem to instead reflect a Brooklyn Democrat’s idea of blue-collar voters. I asked Katz about his outsider candidates appealing mostly to people inside the Democratic tent. First, he disputed the premise of the question. Then he suggested that his candidates’ struggles are the result of being outspent on TV. But he was confident that working-class voters will come around eventually. “There’s just a challenging reality that some of this takes work and time,” he said. “It takes a lot of months, a lot of years, to establish fundamental realignments. And what’s occurring is a fundamental realignment. And it might not happen in two months or six months or one cycle, but it’s happening.” K atz’s views reflect a common theory among anti-establishment candidates and consultants on the left and the right. He believes that supermajorities of the population want the same things that he does. The problem, as he sees it, is that billionaires are distracting voters with culture-war issues and preventing working-class people from hearing the populists’ message. Voters do not in fact agree with progressive Democrats on everything. In much of the country, the working class in particular believes that the Democratic Party is out of touch with their values on issues including immigration, DEI policies, and gender. The idea that Democrats can win back the ground they’ve lost to the GOP during the Trump era without addressing that weakness head-on is far-fetched. (It’s not for nothing that the strongest Trump-state electoral overperformers this cycle, based on polling, are moderates, such as Roy Cooper in North Carolina and Mary Peltola in Alaska. El-Sayed, by contrast, appears to be an underperformer. A recent poll gave Michigan’s establishment-Democratic candidate for governor a 12.4-point lead, compared with just a 2.5-point lead for El-Sayed.) And if they don’t become competitive in more places, then they won’t have the political power to pass the kinds of populist reforms that Katz so badly wants to see—a fact that Katz acknowledges. “What defines the vision is a desire for real power that can fundamentally change the trajectory we’re currently on,” he said. “What that requires is winning a lot of hard elections in a lot of places and making those in positions of power better.” Recent polls suggest that Democrats have as much as a nine-point advantage on the generic ballot. In that environment, even weak candidates who lack broad appeal could win. The real way to evaluate Katz’s candidates will be to compare their margin of victory with the overall results. [ Marc Novicoff: How the polls could be wrong again ] I asked Katz if there was anything that could convince him that his approach is wrong—that progressive candidates really do need to moderate on certain social issues to win hard contests. He seemed confused by the question. “I don’t necessarily have an easy, like—that’s what we have elections for.” I tried again. What if El-Sayed does not win in Michigan, and voters say that’s because he seems too close with Hasan Piker, the Communist-sympathizing Twitch streamer? Would that change your perspective? “I think Abdul is going to win,” he said. I waited, and Katz kept riffing. “I think about politics a lot like sports, in the sense that anyone who’s trying to be good at the job watches a lot of tape.” Just as coaches add new wrinkles to their offense during the offseason, he’ll review the midterm results and make changes for 2028. It was a convenient way to avoid answering the question. So I asked what he’s learned from this midterm cycle, one in which a scandal-plagued populist candidate has already dropped out and others are polling worse than their moderate-Democrat peers. “Well, I want to see what happens in November,” Katz replied. As the election approached, Katz and I kept in touch, and he began to joke more frequently about leaving politics. He said it so often that I started to wonder if he was serious. Yes, he spends much of his time writing scripts and staging scenes—as he’d always intended—but he seems miserable. Katz assured me that he really was just kidding and has no plans to find a new line of work. Depending on how the midterms go, he might want to reconsider. *Illustration Sources: Adam Gray / Bloomberg / Getty; Angelina Katsanis / AFP / Getty; Eleanor Dearman / Fort Worth Star-Telegram / Tribune News Service / Getty; Joe Raedle / Getty.

items.title: The Backlash to Corruption Is Going Global
items.description: N icole Irvin voted for Donald Trump three times because she thought he had business savvy and appreciated that he was politically incorrect. “I like his roughness,” she told me. I met her in the parking lot of a Walmart Supercenter in Levittown, Pennsylvania, a planned suburban community in the state’s First Congressional District, a midterm battleground. She used to get her news from the right-wing commentator Candace Owens, and she cried when Charlie Kirk was killed last year. Lately, though, she has tuned out the GOP’s messaging because it is so discordant with her own experience. She had just paid $10 for a phone charger—her son had broken her old one—and recalled when she paid half that much. “I asked the lady, ‘Is there any clearance section?’” The cost was significant because Irvin, who works at a tire-repair company, lives paycheck to paycheck. Meanwhile she sees politicians protecting their own wealth, and she can’t remember the greed ever being so blatant as under Trump. “They all make deals with each other,” she said. Corruption is topping voter concerns in recent polls, dominating Democratic messaging, and forcing Republicans to play defense in red states. If that marks a sharp shift from recent American elections, in which such allegations have played a relatively minor role, it mirrors a growing global trend. Around the world, a backlash against corruption has roused voters and undercut populist, right-wing politicians. Now it may play a decisive role in the midterm elections. I first noticed this in Hungary earlier this year. Viktor Orbán, an ally of President Trump and a model for his MAGA movement, was ousted in April after 16 years in power. I asked his former political director, Balázs Orbán—who is not related to the former prime minister—whether he saw parallels between the campaign that cost his boss his job and the contest that could end Republican control of Congress. Like Trump, the long-serving prime minister had confronted corruption accusations in previous elections, but won anyway. “Why is that?” Orbán asked me. “It’s because of the economy. If people feel the economy is going in a good direction, they say, ‘Okay, there are some rich people, but we are also doing well.’” As Orbán sees it, these were the terms of a basic social contract. “The problem right now is that since people don’t feel that they are doing well, they want politicians to keep the social agreement: that if we suffer, we should suffer together.” The effects of this backlash could be equally dramatic in the United States, where perceptions of government corruption hit a record high this year, according to Gallup. On this metric, the U.S. now outpaces most other advanced economies. If MAGA meets the same fate in the midterms as other entrenched right-wing parties have around the world, it would suggest that history is moving in a new, and unpredictable, direction. The end of the Cold War brought the spread of Western-style liberal democracy. Then, in the 2010s, nationalism, authoritarian populism, and crony capitalism—features of Vladimir Putin’s Russia—surged in popularity, as the historian Timothy Snyder has argued. In Hungary and Serbia, countries that lie at the seam of East and West, the balance has now tipped back toward liberal democracy. The same could happen this autumn in America. A s global wealth disparities widen, a common dynamic keeps playing out in nation after nation. Nearly two years of student-led anti-corruption protests in Serbia helped dislodge the country’s strongman leader, Aleksandar Vučić, in elections last weekend. In Brazil, voter discontent with seedy politics may have worked in the incumbent’s favor. Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva beat back a challenge from Flávio Bolsonaro, who is being investigated for alleged money laundering and tax evasion. In Israel, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu might hold on to power after messy coalition talks, but he was weakened by long-standing accusations of bribery and fraud. Anti-corruption demonstrations in India have rattled that country’s nationalist strongman leader, Narendra Modi, after more than 12 years in power. It’s not hard to understand why the ostentatious behavior of political elites would be more galling during a cost-of-living crisis. The three most important issues to voters in Hungary, according to opinion research , were cost of living and inflation; public services, including health care and education; and corruption and governance. “The government is there to benefit the authoritarian leader’s friends,” a retired butcher I met outside Budapest told me, “and we all pay the price.” By the end of Orbán’s tenure, his son-in-law and childhood best friend had become among the richest men in the country. The opposition party, which won a supermajority in Parliament and put its leader, Péter Magyar, in the prime minister’s office, framed corruption as a form of theft. “The money that is stolen,” Magyar argued, should be funding pensions and child-welfare services. Candidates in the United States are trying to make a similar connection. “We have an affordability crisis because we have a corruption crisis,” James Talarico, the Democratic Senate candidate in Texas, has said. Jon Ossoff, the Democratic incumbent in Georgia, has put it this way: “Prices soar while the president rakes in billions.” The people around Trump have also done well. Look no further than his youngest son, the 20-year-old Barron, a college student whose estimated net worth stands at about $150 million, mostly derived from the family’s cryptocurrency company. The president’s own net worth is estimated to have grown by about $2.7 billion since the start of his second term, and is up to approximately $7 billion. [ Read: The watchdogs are barking themselves hoarse ] As in Hungary, corruption has moved to the top of the agenda for Americans. A recent Fox News poll found that government corruption drew the most concern among voters, above inflation and gas prices. And it’s changing voters’ minds. Irvin, the Pennsylvania voter, isn’t planning to cast a ballot at all on Tuesday. Her abstention, given her past voting habits, is a loss for the Republican incumbent, Representative Brian Fitzpatrick, a former FBI agent. Perhaps sensing the potency of the corruption issue, Fitzpatrick has tried to use it against his Democratic challenger, Bob Harvie, a county commissioner. Campaign signs just beyond the Walmart parking lot allege that Harvie voted to give himself a pay raise. (In 2022, the bipartisan county board approved small cost-of-living adjustments for county officials, set to take effect after the next election.) Fitzpatrick’s campaign didn’t respond to a request for comment. Harvie, a former social-studies teacher, recently held his ninth town hall. Consistently, the two main issues raised by voters have been costs and corruption, he told me. “People are finally lashing out against a government that isn’t working for them,” he said. The pain is especially acute now because residents have just gotten their first shipment of heating oil. The pattern at campaign events is for voters to ask him about their “astronomical” heating bill, and then the very next question will be: How are we going to change Washington and stop this corruption? [ From the October 2026 issue: MAGA is making the world safe for corruption ] I asked Orbán, who badly wants the Republicans to win, what the party could do to tamp down voter concerns. Perhaps, I suggested, the president could try to minimize grift or the appearance of it. After all, he’s building a gilded ballroom while average diesel prices exceed $6 a gallon. Orbán laughed. “My advice would be to attack the Democrats,” he said. “They are trying to portray themselves as moderates, but they are not honest.” That’s the approach that many Republicans are taking. The problem is that a similar strategy already failed in Hungary. Gabby Deutch and Madison Hahamy contributed reporting.

items.title: Six in seven journalist murders go unpunished, UNESCO reports
items.description: Global impunity for journalist killings has risen for the first time in more than a decade, while the growing use of drones is an emerging threat for reporters in conflict zones, according to the latest report from UN cultural organization UNESCO.

items.title: Pedro Sánchez: “España no se gobierna desde Washington, Tel Aviv, Moscú o Buenos Aires”
items.description: El presidente del Gobierno, Pedro Sánchez, ha advertido este lunes del riesgo de “retroceso” en las libertades conquistadas por el avance de las fuerzas de extrema derecha y ha llamado a construir una “Europa más fuerte, más autónoma y más unida” en su discurso en el foro World in Progress (WIP), organizado por el Grupo PRISA en Bacelona . items.title: Pakistan fined for slow over-rate in tri-series final
items.description: Pakistan have been fined five per cent of their match fees for maintaining a slow over-rate during their three-wicket victory over Sri Lanka in the One-day International tri-series final in Lahore on Saturday. The hosts were found to be one over short after time allowances were taken into consideration by match referee Jeff Crowe of the Emirates ICC Elite Panel, the International Cricket Council said in a statement on Monday. Pakistan captain Shaheen Shah Afridi pleaded guilty to the offence and accepted the proposed sanction, which was imposed under Article 2.22 of the ICC Code of Conduct for Players and Player Support Personnel. The provision stipulates a fine of five per cent of a player’s match fee for every over his side fails to bowl within the allotted time. The charge was levelled by on-field umpires Ahsan Raza and Wayne Knights, third umpire Sharfuddoula Ibne Shahid and fourth umpire Rashid Riaz. Pakistan had conceded 325-8 in the final before chasing down the target of 326 with three wickets and nine balls to spare, securing the tri-series title in front of their home crowd at Gaddafi Stadium. Fakhar Zaman led the successful chase with 127 off 99 balls, hitting 11 fours and six sixes to register his 12th ODI century. His innings helped Pakistan recover from an early collapse and complete a joint-record successful chase in an ODI final.

items.title: Musique gospel : Élisée W. Tiendrebeogo dévoile son premier album « BoenzemWende »
items.description: L’artiste gospel, Élisée W. Tiendrebeogo, a procédé au lancement officiel de son tout premier album, intitulé « BoenzemWende », composé de 12 titres, le dimanche 1er novembre 2026 à Ouagadougou. À cette occasion, il a également présenté un clip vidéo extrait de cette œuvre musicale. C’est au rythme de sonorités empreintes de reconnaissance et d’action de grâce que l’artiste gospel Élisée W. Tiendrebeogo a présenté au public son premier album, après neuf années d’écriture, de réflexion, d’inspiration et de maturation artistique. Intitulé « BoenzemWende », cet album de 12 titres porte un message de foi, d’espérance et de reconnaissance envers Dieu. Un extrait du clip vidéo Selon l’artiste, le choix de ce titre en langue mooré, qui signifie « Rien n’est comparable à Dieu », traduit sa volonté de valoriser son identité culturelle tout en magnifiant la puissance divine. « Nous avons voulu que ce titre soit en mooré pour marquer notre identité. Nous sommes Burkinabè. À travers ce chant et cet album, nous voulons adresser un message à toute personne qui traverse une situation particulière : la grâce de Dieu est toujours disponible. Rien ne lui est impossible », a-t-il expliqué. À travers les différentes compositions, l’artiste aborde plusieurs thématiques de la vie quotidienne et spirituelle. L’artiste gospel évoque notamment le travail bien fait, l’accompagnement des enfants, le mariage ainsi que l’action de grâce. Il lance particulièrement un appel aux aînés et aux personnes ressources à soutenir les enfants, qu’il considère comme l’avenir de demain. Une vue des participants « Nous encourageons la jeunesse au travail bien fait, car Dieu bénit l’œuvre de nos mains. Nous invitons également nos aînés à apporter un soutien infaillible et inconditionnel aux enfants, parce qu’ils sont l’avenir de demain », a souligné Élisée W. Tiendrebeogo. Revenant sur le processus de réalisation de l’album, Élisée W. Tiendrebeogo a indiqué que cette œuvre, mûrie pendant neuf ans, est le fruit d’un travail collectif. Pour lui, les douze titres constituent autant de témoignages et de messages destinés à fortifier la foi des auditeurs. Élisée W. Tiendrebeogo explique que son œuvre traduit sa reconnaissance envers Dieu « Ma prière est que cet album touche, édifie, fortifie et fasse grandir la foi de chaque personne qui va l’écouter », a-t-il confié. Il invite par ailleurs le public à découvrir les douze compositions, en prenant le temps de s’imprégner du message porté par chacune d’elles. « Ce sont douze témoignages différents, douze messages. Même si vous écoutez un titre par mois, cela me va déjà », a lancé M. Tiendrebeogo L’album « BoenzemWende » est disponible au prix de 5 000 F CFA. Le clip vidéo est également accessible sur la chaîne YouTube de l’artiste, Élisée W. Tiendrebeogo. Débutant ses premiers pas dans le ministère musical à l’âge de 12 ans au sein de l’école du dimanche de l’Église de l’Alliance chrétienne, Élisée W. Tiendrebeogo s’est progressivement illustré sur la scène musicale. En 2013, il est lauréat d’Alliance Academy. En 2014, il remporte le concours La Harpe de l’Excellence, où il est désigné meilleur chantre masculin. En 2018, il confirme son engagement musical en devenant lauréat de Faso Academy. Parallèlement à sa carrière artistique, il poursuit des études de médecine. Sakinatou ZOUNDI Minute.bf

items.title: Maroc : un jeune dessinateur lourdement condamné pour avoir caricaturé Mohammed VI
items.description: Yasser Mounbir, un jeune dessinateur marocain de 22 ans, a été lourdement condamné à 4 ans de prison ferme et une amende de 40 000 dirhams pour « insulte à l’encontre du roi » Mohammed VI et « insultes envers des agents de l’Etat ». Le verdict a été prononcé vendredi 30 octobre par un tribunal de Casablanca, contre le dessinateur qui avait publié sur Instagram des caricatures de Mohammed VI. Les avocats de Yasser Mounbir qui était placé en détention provisoire depuis le mois de juin 2026, ont annoncé faire appel de ce verdict jugé « disproportionné ». L’Association marocaine des droits humains (AMDH) a demandé la libération du jeune artiste. Une pétition en ligne a été lancée par le collectif Free Yasser, pour réclamer sa libération. Le comité de soutien du dessinateur, cité par le journal Le Monde, dénonce « une tendance regrettable d’intimidation et de criminalisation de la liberté d’expression ». Le comité de soutien souligne dans sa pétition que « l’art n’est pas un crime. La liberté de créer est un droit fondamental garanti par la constitution marocaine ». Le Maroc condamne un jeune dessinateur pour avoir caricaturé le roi Au Maroc, la « diffamation, l'insulte ou l'atteinte à la vie privée du roi » sont passibles de six mois à deux ans de prison Plusieurs journalistes et artistes ont été emprisonnés au Maroc. C’est le cas du rappeur Tarek Tazi, connu sous le nom artistique de T-Flow. Il a été condamné, en septembre dernier par un tribunal de Fès, à 11 mois de prison ferme pour avoir critiqué les politiques du gouvernement. Au-delà des artistes, la répression s’abat sur toutes les voix discordantes au Maroc. En 2023, Saïd Boukidoud a été condamné à 5 ans de prison ferme pour avoir critiqué la normalisation des relations diplomatiques avec Israël. items.title: Binance reanuda las retiradas de fondos tras el histórico robo y los clientes sacan 4.700 millones de dólares
items.description: Binance, la mayor plataforma cripto del planeta, ha reactivado paulatinamente sus servicios tras sufrir el mayor hackeo de la historia de la industria de activos digitales. El exchange , que informó del incidente a última hora del jueves, se vio obligado a suspender temporalmente las retiradas de fondos de sus clientes para reforzar la seguridad y contener una posible fuga masiva de capital. Sin embargo, este domingo comenzó a reactivar el servicio de forma gradual, a medida que completaba las comprobaciones de seguridad necesarias. En las primeras horas, las retiradas se dispararon y la plataforma registró salidas por valor de 4.700 millones de dólares hasta la mañana de este lunes, según confirmó un portavoz a Bloomberg. La empresa, en paralelo, trabaja para congelar los activos robados por los atacantes. Seguir leyendo

items.title: Pr Adjima Thiombiano: «Si le Burkina ne leur convient pas, qu’ils repartent d’où ils viennent…»
items.description: Ce lundi 2 novembre 2026 à l’immeuble de l’éducation, les travailleurs du Ministère de l’Enseignement Supérieur, de la Recherche et de l’Innovation et du Ministère de l’Enseignement de Base, de l’Alphabétisation et de la Promotion des Langues nationales étaient mobilisés pour la traditionnelle montée des couleurs nationales. La cérémonie était présidée par les deux ministres, les camarades Pr Adjima THIOMBIANO et Jacques Sosthène DINGARA. Au cours de cette cérémonie, le ministre chargé de l’enseignement supérieur qui a livré le message du mois, a réagi suite à des propos malveillants tenus par des nouveaux bacheliers de la diaspora sur le Burkina Faso sur les réseaux sociaux la semaine dernière. «Si le Burkina ne leur convient pas qu’ils repartent d’où ils viennent…nous sommes très fiers d’être des Burkinabè et nous nous battons toujours pour que le Burkina soit meilleur» a réagi le camarade Pr Adjima THIOMBIANO. Le ministre chargé de l’enseignement supérieur s’est voulu clair: «Que ce soit dans le cadre du Pacte NEKRE, que ce soit dans la nouvelle dynamique impulsée par les plus hautes autorités de ce pays, il n’y aura aucune chance à qui que ce soit, d’où qu’ils viennent de venir perturber notre système éducatif. Chacun de vous devra s’ériger en rempart face à des comportements qui frisent souvent la révolte. Chacun devrait ressentir cette fierté de revenir apprendre chez lui et de créer des conditions idéales pour que chacun puisse véritablement être fier», a poursuivi le Pr Adjima THIOMBIANO avant de les mettre en garde contre toute tentative de saper les efforts consentis par les plus hautes autorités pour donner à l’université burkinabè sa lettre de noblesse. «Il n’y aura pas de place pour ces enfants égarés dans nos campus. Nous n’allons pas tolérer que tout ce que nous avons construit en 4 années, que cela soit battu en brêche par ces enfante», a insisté le ministre avant d’ajouter que «Si un enfant quitte ailleurs pour venir étudier chez lui, c’est noble. Nous l’accueillons tant que les intentions sont bonnes. Mais un enfant qui vient pour dénigrer ce pays, il trouvera tous les Burkinabè sur son chemin», a-t-il laissé entendre. Toujours sur le plan de l’éducation, le Pr Adjima THIOMBIANO est revenu sur le lancement le 17 octobre 2026 à Kaya, du Pacte NEKRÉ pour la Refondation de l’école burkinabè. Il a invité l’ensemble des acteurs à plus d’engagement afin de faire de ce Pacte qui consacre définitivement la cohérence du système éducatif depuis le préscolaire jusqu’à l’université, «pour qu’il ait cette renaissance réelle de l’école burkinabè». Mais avant, le ministre a tenu à souhaiter un joyeux anniversaire aux Forces Armées Nationales qui ont célébré hier 1er novembre 2026, leur 66è anniversaire. Il leur a exprimé sa gratitude et toute sa fierté «pour le combat que ces hommes et ces femmes mènent, abattent au quotidien pour que le Burkina puisse rester encore débout», a indiqué le camarade Pr Adjima THIOMBIANO. DCRP-MESRI L’article Pr Adjima Thiombiano: «Si le Burkina ne leur convient pas, qu’ils repartent d’où ils viennent…» est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Kindia : les vendeuses manifestent contre le manque de places dans les marchés et interpellent Doumbouya
items.description: La tension monte à Kindia. Les vendeuses du grand marché et d’autres marchés de la commune urbaine sont descendues dans les rues ce lundi 2 novembre 2026 pour dénoncer le manque de places disponibles dans les infrastructures marchandes construites dans le cadre du contrat de bail des marchés. Elles interpellent directement le président Mamadi Doumbouya pour une intervention urgente. La mobilisation a débuté au centre-ville, où les manifestantes ont érigé des barricades, perturbant la circulation sur plusieurs axes routiers avant de rallier la devanture de la mairie. Elles dénoncent notamment les conditions d’attribution des espaces commerciaux et accusent les autorités communales de ne pas apporter de réponse satisfaisante à leurs préoccupations. Porte-parole des manifestantes, Yalakhan Soumah a expliqué les raisons de leur colère. « Nous sommes sorties pour dénoncer cette politique de bail de nos marchés par nos autorités. Ces autorités ne sont pas bonnes. Elles ont mis tous nos marchés en bail en construisant des étages, et une vendeuse de piment ne peut pas prendre une boutique pour revendre. Les femmes de Kindia n'ont pas de place. C'est pourquoi nous demandons urgemment au président Mamadi Doumbouya de faire face à notre situation », a-t-elle déclaré. Face à la mobilisation, les forces de défense et de sécurité sont intervenues pour échanger avec les manifestantes et tenter d'obtenir le dégagement des barricades. Une démarche qui a été partiellement suivie d'effet. De son côté, le maire de la commune urbaine de Kindia, Elhadj Aboubacar Molota Camara, attend un retour au calme avant de s'exprimer officiellement sur cette situation. Munies de pancartes, certaines manifestantes continuaient d'occuper plusieurs axes de la ville, tandis que d'autres ont pris la direction de la résidence du préfet de Kindia. Aboubacar Dramé, correspondant régional à Kindia L’article Kindia : les vendeuses manifestent contre le manque de places dans les marchés et interpellent Doumbouya est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: On eve of midterms, final polls point to Democratic gains, but can Republicans hold the Senate?
items.description: Democrats have made significant gains in the final days of the 2026 midterm campaign, with new polls showing them leading in several states that President Donald Trump carried in 2024. The findings point to a changing political landscape, although the outcome of the Senate contests remains uncertain. The final New York Times /Siena College surveys of seven key Senate battlegrounds show Democratic candidates ahead in Michigan , Texas, Kansas, Maine and Ohio. They also hold narrower leads in Alaska and Iowa, where the contests remain highly competitive. The results have attracted particular attention because several of these states have traditionally favoured Republicans. Democratic leads in Texas and Kansas, in particular, would have appeared unlikely only a few months ago. The surveys, released on November 1, covered 5,708 likely voters across the seven states. The individual state surveys had margins of sampling error ranging from approximately 3.3 to 4.8 percentage points. In Michigan, Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed leads Republican Mike Rogers by 53 to 42 per cent. In Texas, James Talarico is ahead of Republican Ken Paxton, 50 to 43pc. Kansas Democrat Adam Hamilton leads incumbent Republican Senator Roger Marshall, 49 to 44pc, while in Maine, Democrat Troy Jackson leads Republican Senator Susan Collins, 51 to 45pc. Ohio presents another potentially significant contest. Former Democratic senator Sherrod Brown leads Republican Jon Husted, 49 to 44pc. The margins are narrower in Alaska and Iowa. Mary Peltola leads Republican Senator Dan Sullivan, 48 to 46pc, while Democrat Josh Turek is ahead of Republican Ashley Hinson, 48 to 47pc. Although Democrats lead numerically in all seven surveys, the differences in Alaska and Iowa are too small to establish a statistically reliable advantage. Even the larger leads elsewhere remain subject to polling error. The findings nevertheless show how competitive the Senate map has become as both parties seek control of Congress. A Republican warning: The Senate remains competitive The prospect of Democratic gains is no longer being acknowledged only by Democratic strategists or traditionally liberal media outlets. Fox News , which generally offers a more favourable perspective on Republican electoral prospects, has also revised its assessments. In its November 1 Power Rankings, Fox moved Kansas from “Lean Republican” to “Toss-up”, acknowledging that the Republican incumbent was facing a serious challenge in a traditionally conservative state. Of the 100 seats in the Senate, Fox considers Democrats favoured in 48 Senate seats and Republicans in 45, with seven competitive states likely to determine control of the chamber. It nevertheless describes the overall Senate contest as a toss-up. Its reasoning is based largely on electoral geography. Trump carried seven of the 11 battleground states in 2024, several by double-digit margins. Republicans believe that voters who supported him in those states could return to the polls and support Republican Senate candidates, even if the national political environment has shifted. Fox also points to the number of undecided voters in Alaska, Iowa and Kansas. A late movement towards Republican candidates, combined with strong Election Day participation, could change the outcome. The network’s analysis presents two possible scenarios: a Democratic gain that could give the party as many as 55 Senate seats, or a Republican performance strong enough to preserve a majority of up to 52. Either party needs to secure 51 seats in the Senate for a majority win. The House picture is different. Fox ’s final Power Rankings project that Democrats are likely to win at least 223 seats, with the possibility of reaching 240 in a strong performance. In the lower House of Representatives, the winner needs to gain at least 218 out of the 435 voting seats. Other forecasts examine the changing political map. The Wall Street Journal , reporting on the latest assessment by the Cook Political Report, said Democrats had become slight favourites to capture the Senate. Cook identifies seven Senate races — Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas — as sufficiently competitive to remain within the margin of error. For the House, Cook projects Democratic gains of between 12 and 25 seats, potentially giving the party a majority of as many as 240 members. Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Dr. Abdul El-Sayed greets supporters at the “Knock Out the Vote Rally” on November 1, 2026 in Southfield, Michigan. —Getty Images via AFP CBS News has also reported a sustained Democratic advantage in its House modelling. Its October 25 analysis, however, offered an important qualification: the Democratic lead had remained relatively stable rather than expanding, and voters who were still uncertain about participating tended to lean more Republican. That distinction matters. A favourable polling environment does not necessarily mean that all voters expressing dissatisfaction with the administration will turn out on Election Day. The Harvard model assigns probabilities to a possible Democratic takeover. A forecast from the Harvard ElectIt project offers another way of assessing the congressional contests. The project provides three versions of its 2026 forecast: one based on its statistical election model, a second incorporating national generic-ballot polling and a third incorporating available state and district polls. The underlying LogisTiCC model uses historical congressional election results and accounts for factors including incumbency, candidate-specific effects, strategic departures from office and the historical tendency of the president’s party to lose ground in midterm elections. The poll-based versions adjust the model using additional polling information. Under the forecast configuration displayed in the Harvard link used for this report, Democrats have a 96pc probability of taking the House and a 79pc probability of gaining control of the Senate. The model projects approximately 241 Democratic House seats, a net gain of 26, and 53 Democratic Senate seats, an increase of six. The reported 95pc ranges are wide: 214 to 282 seats in the House and 47 to 57 in the Senate. These ranges underline that the figures are statistical estimates, not guaranteed outcomes. The Senate projection is particularly significant because it illustrates how the model evaluates the possibility of Democrats overcoming the geographical disadvantages that have traditionally made the chamber difficult for them to capture. The Harvard project cautions against treating a single projected seat count as a certain result. Its different forecast versions can produce different estimates as polling information changes. Progressive politics and the changing Democratic coalition The emerging political picture also reflects a longer evolution within the Democratic Party, particularly the growth of progressive politics and dissatisfaction with established political institutions. Commentator Zeeshan Shah, a physician in Northern Virginia, believes Senator Bernie Sanders helped inject new energy into the progressive movement, creating political space for candidates challenging the Republican establishment. After Sanders came New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani , who is believed to have taken that energy into the mainstream by directly challenging Trump and the politics associated with his administration, according to Mohsin Masood, a Virginia educationist. Political science professor Farhat Haq believes Democrats could benefit from another pendulum swing in American politics, driven largely by dissatisfaction with Trump. US President Donald Trump arrives to speak at a midterm campaign rally at Five Flags Center in Dubuque, Iowa on November 1, 2026. —AFP She points to rising living costs, the war involving Iran and the Gaza conflict as factors contributing to public discontent. Haq links the economic consequences of the Iran war to inflation and the pressure on household budgets. She also argues that Trump has lost support among some of the groups that helped him politically, including Latino voters . Haq notes that PTI supporters in the United States, despite remaining politically active, are no longer supporting Trump as they did previously. Together, these assessments suggest that the political shift may reflect more than the immediate circumstances of the campaign. Economic anxiety, foreign-policy disagreements and disappointment with established political leadership have all entered the debate over the direction of the country. The final test comes on Tuesday Republicans currently hold a 53-47 Senate majority, including two independents who caucus with Democrats. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to secure an outright 51-seat majority. The House is a more straightforward target. Republicans hold a narrow majority, and the latest polling and election ratings point to a highly competitive contest for control. A change in either chamber would significantly affect Trump’s ability to advance his legislative programme. Democratic control would also give the opposition party greater authority to investigate the administration and scrutinise its policies. The final polls and forecasts show Democrats entering Election Day with opportunities in several states and congressional districts that were not widely expected to be competitive earlier in the campaign. Yet polling error cannot be dismissed. Undecided voters, differences in turnout and the difficulty of predicting who will actually vote can all produce results that diverge from final surveys. For Democrats, the election offers an opportunity to regain the House and potentially the Senate as well. For Republicans, the task is to persuade their supporters that the contests remain open and to ensure that voters who have not participated early turn out on Tuesday. The final results will show whether the patterns identified by the polls and forecasting models were temporary expressions of dissatisfaction or evidence of a broader change in American electoral politics.

items.title: Déguerpissements à Okala, Diba-Diba et Lac Bleu : Immongault précise les mesures d’accompagnement
items.description: À trois jours du démarrage des travaux routiers annoncé pour le 4 novembre, le gouvernement affine les modalités de prise en charge des populations concernées par les opérations de libération des emprises à Okala, Diba-Diba et Lac Bleu. Indemnisations, scolarité, accompagnement social et attribution de parcelles étaient au cœur d’une réunion présidée, le 1er novembre, par le vice-président du gouvernement, Hermann Immongault. Un instant des travaux, le 1er novembre 2026. © Com. VPG Le gouvernement veut éviter que les opérations de déguerpissement liées au projet d’aménagement routier dans le Grand Libreville ne se limitent à la libération des emprises. Le vice-président du gouvernement, Hermann Immongault, a réuni, dimanche 1er novembre 2026, les membres de l’équipe gouvernementale concernés, la gouverneure de l’Estuaire ainsi que les maires d’Akanda et du premier arrondissement de Libreville, pour faire le point sur la situation des ménages impactés. Les échanges ont notamment porté sur les mesures de prise en charge financière, la continuité de la scolarité des enfants, l’accompagnement social et l’attribution de parcelles. Les zones concernées sont notamment Okala, sur le tronçon allant du dispensaire à la centrale SEEG, ainsi que les axes Lac Bleu-Diba-Diba. Cette rencontre intervient après la conférence de presse du 30 octobre, au cours de laquelle le porte-parole du gouvernement, Emmanuel Eyeghe Nze, et les ministres concernés avaient entrepris de rassurer les populations sur les conditions de déroulement de l’opération. Des populations identifiées, des emprises réévaluées Quelques ministres présents lors des travaux. © Com. VPG Selon les précisions apportées par la gouverneure de l’Estuaire, les populations directement concernées ont été identifiées et invitées à se rapprocher des services compétents pour obtenir leurs fiches de valorisation des impacts. «Les populations impactées sont clairement identifiées. Et depuis la semaine dernière, elles passent pour saisir les fiches de valorisation de l’impact» , a-t-elle indiqué. Les autorités sont également revenues sur les inquiétudes suscitées par le marquage des habitations à Okala. Les premiers tracés, matérialisés en rouge, reposaient sur une emprise jugée trop large. Après réévaluation technique, celle-ci a été ramenée à 30 mètres. «Les derniers marquages sont des marquages de couleur différente qui ont été apposés sur les murs des maisons des personnes impliquées réellement dans le projet» , a précisé la gouverneure. Concilier travaux publics et impératifs sociaux À travers ce suivi rapproché, l’exécutif entend concilier les impératifs de modernisation du réseau routier, de fluidification du trafic et les préoccupations des ménages appelés à quitter leurs habitations. Le démarrage des travaux étant annoncé pour le 4 novembre, l’enjeu est désormais de rendre effectives les mesures d’accompagnement annoncées, afin que cette opération d’aménagement urbain ne se traduise pas par une aggravation de la précarité des populations concernées. L’article Déguerpissements à Okala, Diba-Diba et Lac Bleu : Immongault précise les mesures d’accompagnement est apparu en premier sur Gabonreview.com | Actualité du Gabon | .

items.title: Sahara occidental : Rabat veut faire radier le statut de territoire non autonome
items.description: Après le veto russe au Conseil de sécurité vendredi 30 octobre, Rabat entend déplacer son offensive diplomatique vers l'Assemblée générale, en ciblant prioritairement le Comité des 24 (C-24) et la Quatrième Commission. L'objectif est désormais d'obtenir le retrait du Sahara occidental de la liste des territoires non autonomes, sur laquelle il figure depuis 1963. D’emblée, il convient de rappeler que les Nations unies ne reconnaissent pas le Maroc comme puissance administrante du territoire. Cette absence de reconnaissance prive Rabat de tout fondement juridique lui permettant de présenter son contrôle territorial comme une administration internationalement reconnue. La stratégie du Maroc pour s’accaparer du Sahara occidental Pour parvenir à ses fins, le Maroc compte convertir les soutiens bilatéraux obtenus en faveur de son plan d'autonomie en une majorité multilatérale susceptible de soutenir une initiative de radiation. Cette stratégie suppose une mobilisation diplomatique tous azimuts. Rabat cherchera à obtenir des engagements de vote, des parrainages de textes et le soutien du plus grand nombre de délégations, notamment en Afrique, dans les Caraïbes, en Asie et dans le Pacifique. Les partenaires européens et américains seront également sollicités pour convaincre les États hésitants. Dans ce contexte, Rabat misera prioritairement sur le soutien des États-Unis, du lobby juif AIPAC, d’Israël et de la France. Il cherchera également à mobiliser ses relais d’influence, notamment à Washington, tout en recourant à ses méthodes habituelles de marchandage diplomatique, fondées sur les incitations financières (diplomatie du chéquier) et l’instrumentalisation de ses ressources en phosphates. La procédure comporte toutefois plusieurs étapes distinctes. Le C-24, organe subsidiaire de l'Assemblée générale, examine la situation des territoires non autonomes et formule des recommandations. La Quatrième Commission examine notamment son rapport et transmet ses recommandations à l'Assemblée générale plénière. C'est cette dernière qui détient la compétence décisionnelle concernant le maintien ou le retrait d'un territoire de la liste. Une majorité favorable au Maroc au C-24 ou à la Quatrième Commission ne suffirait donc pas, à elle seule, à obtenir la radiation. Le pari marocain repose sur l'absence de droit de veto à l'Assemblée générale et sur la possibilité de constituer une majorité de circonstance. Mais Rabat devra surmonter une difficulté politique majeure : le soutien au plan d'autonomie ne signifie pas nécessairement adhésion à la souveraineté marocaine, encore moins approbation du retrait du territoire de la liste des territoires non autonomes. Plusieurs États soutiennent la proposition marocaine comme base de négociation tout en maintenant leur attachement au droit à l'autodétermination et au processus de décolonisation. L'obstacle est également juridique. La résolution 1514 (XV) consacre le droit des peuples coloniaux à l'autodétermination. La résolution 1541 (XV) prévoit trois modalités d'accession à une pleine autonomie politique : l'indépendance, la libre association et l'intégration. Ces options doivent reposer sur l'expression libre et authentique de la volonté des populations concernées. Or, le plan d'autonomie marocain n'a jamais fait l'objet d'une consultation permettant d'établir cette volonté. Les reconnaissances diplomatiques et les déclarations de soutien ne sauraient se substituer à cette exigence. Un autre élément important fragilise la démarche marocaine. Le 15 octobre 2026, le Maroc a voté en faveur du projet de résolution A/C.4/81/L.4, adopté par 152 voix contre deux, avec sept abstentions. Obstacles majeurs à franchir Ce texte réaffirme le droit à l'autodétermination, demande au C-24 de poursuivre l'examen du Sahara occidental et sollicite un nouveau rapport du Secrétaire général à la 82e session. Rabat a donc soutenu une résolution qui maintient explicitement le territoire dans le dispositif onusien de décolonisation. La contre-mobilisation de l'Algérie, du Front Polisario et des États attachés au processus de décolonisation constituera un autre facteur de résistance. Ils pourront notamment s'appuyer sur la continuité des résolutions onusiennes, l'absence de consultation des Sahraouis et les compétences propres de l'Assemblée générale. Parallèlement, la contestation américaine du mandat du C-24, motivée par son prétendu caractère obsolète, le gaspillage de ressources et la duplication des travaux, pourrait servir certains objectifs marocains. La suppression ou la modification du mandat du Comité resterait toutefois subordonnée à une décision de l’Assemblée générale. L’article Sahara occidental : Rabat veut faire radier le statut de territoire non autonome est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Kindia : Des vendeurs au grand marché manifestznt contre le bail des espaces commerciaux
items.description: Les commerçantes du Grand Marché de Kindia et d’autres marchés de la commune urbaine ont exprimé leur dans les rues de Kindia ce lundi matin. À travers une manifestation marquée par des barricades et des perturbations de la circulation, les protestataires ont dénoncé les conditions de mise en bail des infrastructures des marchés et réclamé des espaces commerciaux accessibles à toutes les catégories de vendeuses. Très tôt dans la matinée, les manifestantes ont investi plusieurs artères du centre-ville, où elles ont érigé des barricades pour faire entendre leurs revendications. Elles ont ensuite convergé vers la mairie de Kindia avant de poursuivre leur mobilisation en direction de la résidence du préfet. Au cœur de leur mécontentement figure la réorganisation des marchés et la mise en location des boutiques et magasins aménagés dans le cadre du contrat de bail. Selon les protestataires, les coûts de location seraient hors de portée de nombreuses petites commerçantes, notamment celles qui vivent de la vente de produits alimentaires et de condiments. Prenant la parole au nom des manifestantes, Yalakhan Soumah a vivement critiqué cette politique de gestion des marchés. Elle a estimé que les nouvelles infrastructures ne répondent pas aux réalités économiques des femmes qui exercent de petites activités commerciales. « Nous sommes sorties pour dénoncer cette politique de bail de nos marchés par nos autorités. Elles ont mis tous nos marchés en bail en construisant des étages, et une vendeuse de piment ne peut pas prendre une boutique pour revendre. Les femmes de Kindia n’ont pas de place. C’est pourquoi nous demandons urgemment au président Mamadi Doumbouya de faire face à notre situation », a-t-elle déclaré. De leur côté, certaines manifestantes ont scandé des slogans hostiles à la gestion communale, notamment : « Commune zéro, maire zéro ! Le marché de Kindia n’est pas à bailler ! Nous voulons notre marché et nos places ! » Des pancartes portant des messages de soutien au président de la République, Mamadi Doumbouya, et de rejet du bail des marchés ont également été brandies. La présidente des vendeuses et commerçantes du Grand Marché, Hadja Marie Avaria, a également dénoncé la situation, estimant que les femmes sont les principales victimes de cette nouvelle organisation des espaces marchands. Face à la mobilisation, les forces de défense et de sécurité se sont déployées dans les zones concernées. Des échanges ont été engagés avec les protestataires afin de rétablir la circulation et de libérer les voies publiques. Cette intervention a permis le dégagement partiel de certains axes routiers. Pour sa part, le maire de la commune urbaine de Kindia, Elhadj Aboubacar Molota Camara, a préféré attendre le retour au calme avant de se prononcer officiellement sur les revendications des commerçantes. En réclamant l’intervention du chef de l’État, les manifestantes souhaitent obtenir une révision des modalités de gestion des marchés et des mécanismes d’attribution des espaces commerciaux. Leur principale préoccupation reste l’accès aux places de vente, dans des conditions compatibles avec leurs capacités financières. Cette mobilisation relance ainsi le débat sur la gestion des infrastructures marchandes à Kindia, mais surtout sur la nécessité de concilier modernisation des marchés, accessibilité des espaces commerciaux et protection des activités des petites commerçantes.

items.title: Burkina Faso/Montée des couleurs nationales : Pr Adjima THIOMBIANO réagit suite à la sortie de nouveaux bacheliers de la diaspora sur les réseaux sociaux
items.description: Ce lundi 02 novembre 2026 à l’immeuble de l’éducation, les travailleurs du Ministère de l’Enseignement Supérieur, de la Recherche et de l’Innovation et du Ministère de l’Enseignement de Base, de l’Alphabétisation et de la Promotion des Langues nationales étaient mobilisés pour la traditionnelle montée des couleurs nationales. La cérémonie était présidée par les deux ministres, les camarades Pr Adjima THIOMBIANO et Jacques Sosthène DINGARA. Au cours de cette cérémonie, le ministre chargé de l’enseignement supérieur qui a livré le message du mois, a réagi suite à des propos malveillants tenus par des nouveaux bacheliers de la diaspora sur le Burkina Faso sur les réseaux sociaux la semaine dernière. « Si le Burkina ne leur convient pas, qu’ils repartent d’où ils viennent…nous sommes très fiers d’être des burkinabè et nous nous battons toujours pour que le Burkina soit meilleur », a réagi le camarade Pr Adjima THIOMBIANO. Le ministre chargé de l’enseignement supérieur s’est voulu clair : « Que ce soit dans le cadre du Pacte NEKRE, que ce soit dans la nouvelle dynamique impulsée par les plus hautes autorités de ce pays, Il n’y aura aucune chance à qui que ce soit, d’où qu’ils viennent de venir perturber notre système éducatif. Chacun de vous devra s’ériger en rempart face à des comportements qui meublent souvent la révolte. Chacun devrait ressentir cette fierté de revenir apprendre chez lui et de créer des conditions idéales pour que chacun puisse véritablement être fier », a poursuivi le Pr Adjima THIOMBIANO avant de les mettre en garde contre toute tentative de saper les efforts consentis par les plus hautes autorités pour donner à l’université burkinabè sa lettre de noblesse. « Il n’y aura pas de place pour ces enfants égarés dans nos campus. Nous n’allons pas tolérer que tout ce que nous avons construit en 4 années, que cela soit battu en brèche par ces enfants », a insisté le ministre avant d’ajouter que « Si un enfant quitte ailleurs pour venir étudier chez lui, c’est noble. Nous l’accueillons tant que les intentions sont bonnes. Mais un enfant qui vient pour dénigrer ce pays, il trouvera tous les burkinabè sur son chemin », a-t-il laissé entendre. Toujours sur le plan de l’éducation, le Pr Adjima THIOMBIANO est revenu sur le lancement le 17 octobre 2026 à Kaya , du Pacte NEKRÉ pour la Refondation de l’école burkinabè. Il a invité l’ensemble des acteurs à plus d’engagement afin de faire de ce Pacte qui consacre définitivement la cohérence du système éducatif depuis le préscolaire jusqu’à l’université, « pour qu’il y ait cette renaissance réelle de l’école burkinabè ». Mais avant, le ministre a tenu à souhaiter un joyeux anniversaire aux Forces Armées Nationales qui ont célébré hier 1er novembre 2026, leur 66è anniversaire. Il leur a exprimé sa gratitude et toute sa fierté « pour le combat que ces hommes et ces femmes mènent, abattent au quotidien pour que le Burkina puisse rester encore debout », a indiqué le camarade Pr Adjima THIOMBIANO. DCRP-MESRI
